top10_weekly.title: ALS-linked FUS mutation impairs GEMIN5-dependent mRNA recruitment to neuronal late endosomes.
top10_weekly.abstract: Neurons depend on tightly regulated positioning of cellular components to maintain long-distance signaling, but the mechanisms guiding specific mRNAs to distant regions remain unclear. Here, we show that late endosomes function as selective RNA carriers in human motor neurons and uncover the molecular logic guiding their loading. Using APEX2-mediated proximity labeling, we identify the external transcriptome of RAB7A-positive endosomes and find a specific population of mRNAs enriched for endosomal, axonal, and synaptic functions. We find that mRNAs enriched in RAB7A endosomes contain evolutionarily conserved 5'UTRs that act as localization signals, and that the RNA-binding protein GEMIN5 interacts with these regions to promote endosomal RNA recruitment. Finally, we show that there is a conspicuous loss of endosome-associated transcripts in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-associated conditions, accompanied by the mislocalization of GEMIN5 from endosomes. These findings uncover fundamental principles of RNA compartmentalization and highlight endosomal mRNA loading as a vulnerable axis in neuronal homeostasis.

top10_weekly.title: KCNH1 variants associated with neurodevelopmental disorders exhibit prominent gain of function.
top10_weekly.abstract: Pathogenic variants in KCNH1, encoding the human ether-á-go-go voltage-gated potassium channel (EAG1, KV10.1), are associated with the neurodevelopmental disorders Temple-Baraitser syndrome (TBS), Zimmermann-Laband syndrome (ZLS), epileptic encephalopathy, and other undefined neurodevelopmental disorders. Investigating the functional consequences of KCNH1 variants can provide information about molecular and cellular pathophysiological mechanisms and help guide therapeutic directions. In this study, we determined the functional properties of 26 disease-associated KCNH1 variants including three recurrent and six that were previously unpublished. Findings were compared to the wildtype (WT) channel along with six rare population variants. Our approach used automated patch clamp recording of heterologously expressed KCNH1 variants in both the homozygous state (variant alone) and the clinically-relevant heterozygous state (variant co-expressed with WT channels). We also examined the impact of alternative splice isoforms on functional consequences of specific variants. We demonstrated that the majority of disease-associated KCNH1 variants exhibit features consistent with gain-of-function including hyperpolarized voltage-dependence of activation, accelerated activation kinetics, or both that promote hyperpolarization of the resting membrane potential. By contrast, one unique variant discovered previously in an autism cohort had a depolarized voltage-dependence of activation and was associated with a depolarized resting potential in cells. Pharmacological testing of KCNH1 variants demonstrated differences in potency for channel block by imipramine and an investigational non-selective potassium channel blocker (LY97241) for specific variants. Collectively, our findings support gain-of-function as the most common, albeit not exclusive, molecular mechanism underlying KCNH1-related disorders and suggest opportunities for potential therapeutic drug repurposing strategies for these conditions.

top10_weekly.title: Characterization of plasma misfolded superoxide dismutase 1 in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
top10_weekly.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To characterize the dynamics of plasma misfolded superoxide dismutase 1 (mSOD1) and evaluate its utility as a state-dependent biomarker for patient stratification and therapeutic monitoring in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). METHODS: We utilized an SOD1/G93A mouse model and a cohort of 160 ALS patients, including four with SOD1 mutations, 12 with non-SOD1 mutations (C9orf72, TARDBP, FUS, OPTN), and 144 with nongenetic ALS. Chemical precipitation and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay were used to quantify mSOD1 levels in plasma, spinal cord extracts, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Clinical outcomes were assessed by the annual reduction in the revised ALS Functional Rating Scale (ALSFRS-R) score and ventilator-free survival. RESULTS: In mice, plasma mSOD1 increased at the late symptomatic stage with subsequent numerical decline at the humane endpoint, accompanied by progressive motor neuron loss and increasing mSOD1-associated pathology. In humans, mSOD1 was elevated in 100% of SOD1-mutant, 25% of non-SOD1-mutant, and 22.2% of nongenetic ALS patients. Elevation was state-dependent, enriched in patients with moderate disability (ALSFRS-R 17-45). Plasma and CSF mSOD1 levels were correlated across the overall ALS cohort, but this association was no longer significant after exclusion of SOD1-mutant ALS cases. In one tofersen-treated patient, plasma mSOD1 showed rapid, parallel, and sustained reduction with CSF levels. No significant differences in clinical outcomes were observed in nongenetic ALS based on mSOD1 status. INTERPRETATION: Approximately 22% of nongenetic ALS patients exhibit elevated plasma mSOD1, primarily during the moderate disease stage. Plasma mSOD1 is a candidate state-dependent biomarker for biological stratification and may have potential for treatment monitoring.

top10_weekly.title: Decoder-FFPE-seq enables sensitive, genome-wide spatial transcriptomics of archival tissues at single-cell resolution.
top10_weekly.abstract: Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue-compatible spatial transcriptomics (ST) is transforming biology and histopathology, but achieving high sensitivity, genome-wide coverage, single-cell resolution, and researcher accessibility remains challenging. To address these challenges, we here present a dendrimeric DNA coordinate barcoding design for FFPE tissue-adapted spatial RNA sequencing (Decoder-FFPE-seq) by integrating RNA-to-DNA probe conversion with blotting-assisted barcoding. Decoder-FFPE-seq provides single-cell resolution with a >2.6-fold sensitivity increase in whole-transcriptome mouse brain and archived human sample profiling over existing platforms, resolving potential cellular identity of low-abundance genes, finer tissue architecture, and capturing an epithelial-mesenchymal transition-associated signature for prognostic value. With expanded probe libraries, Decoder-FFPE-seq captures long noncoding and viral RNAs, revealing their spatial coregulatory networks with messenger RNAs in oral squamous cell carcinomas (OSCCs). In an OSCC immunotherapy cohort, two CD8+ T cell subpopulations were respectively identified in pre- and postchemoimmunotherapy samples, potentially linked to treatment response. Decoder-FFPE-seq establishes a robust, high-resolution, and accessible framework for sensitive ST profiling of archival tissues in fundamental and translational studies.

top10_weekly.title: FTO Dependent Trim14 m6A Modification Regulates Neuroinflammation in MPTP-Induced Parkinson's Disease Models via the RhoA/ROCK Pathway.
top10_weekly.abstract: Microglia-mediated inflammation is a major contributor to the development of Parkinson's disease (PD) and N6-Methyladenosine (m6A) has been implicated PD. Here, we explored whether m6A modification is associated with microglia-mediated inflammation using MPTP-treated mice and MPP+-exposed BV2 cells. AAV-mediated gene manipulation, immunostaining, and methylated RNA immunoprecipitation-quantitative PCR were used to explore the underlying mechanisms. We found microglial m6A modification decreased and microglial fat mass and obesity-associated protein (FTO) expression increased in BV2 cells treated with MPP+. Knockdown of FTO expression increased Trim14 expression and protected dopaminergic neurons; Trim14 overexpression significantly blocked the activation of RhoA-ROCK pathway. In MPTP-induced mice, FTO upregulation removes m6A modification from Trim14 mRNA, leading to Trim14 downregulation and subsequent activation of the RhoA-ROCK pathway, thereby exacerbating neuroinflammation. The FTO-Trim14 axis represents a potential therapeutic target for PD.

top10_weekly.title: Altered stability of dynamic functional architecture in the co-occurrence of autism spectrum disorder and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder.
top10_weekly.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) frequently co-occur, whereas the underlying neurobiological mechanisms remain largely unexplored. This study aimed to identify alterations in dynamic functional architecture across ASD, ADHD, and their comorbidity. This study selected 287 participants from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange and ADHD-200 datasets, divided into ASD without ADHD (ASD-only), ADHD without ASD (ADHD-only), ASD + ADHD, and typically developing (TD) groups. In this study, we employed dynamic functional stability at the voxel level by measuring the temporal concordance of dynamic functional connectivity (DFC). Furthermore, whole-brain DFC analyses were conducted using clusters with significant stability alterations as seed regions. Group comparisons and correlation analyses were subsequently performed. Our results showed significant group differences in functional stability in the left superior frontal gyrus, orbital part (ORBsup), right pallidum, and left amygdala. Seed-based analyses identified altered DFC variability between the left amygdala and three regions, including the right middle temporal gyrus (MTG), the left insula, and the left superior occipital gyrus (SOG). Notably, DFC variability between the left amygdala and right MTG was significantly negatively correlated with Social Communication Questionnaire (SCQ) scores in the comorbidity group (r = - 0.620, p < 0.01, FDR corrected). From a dynamic perspective, our findings revealed that ASD, ADHD, and their comorbidity exhibited commonanduniquechanges in brain function, thereby enhancing our understanding of the pathogenesis underlying ASD + ADHD.

top10_weekly.title: Multimodal spatial transcriptomics redefines cortical pathology in Huntington's disease.
top10_weekly.abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is caused by CAG expansion in the huntingtin gene (HTT), yet how somatic repeat instability and HTT inclusions relate to selective cell loss in the human brain remains unclear. We have developed a multimodal spatial transcriptomics approach that enables the definition of transcriptional programs with subcellular resolution, somatic CAG repeat lengths, and eight other pathology markers, including HTT inclusions, in every cell of intact brain sections. Imaging 428,173 cells in the control and HD cortex revealed the selective vulnerability of layer 5-6 (L5-6) near-projecting (NP) neurons and L6b deep-layer excitatory neurons, which undergo a >50% loss that is closely linked to large somatic repeat expansions (>450 ± 55 CAGs). Intranuclear inclusions were most prevalent at intermediate somatic repeat expansions (250-350 CAGs) and were associated with broader transcriptional changes than somatic repeat expansion alone. These data provide a comprehensive resource and establish a general framework for connecting repeat expansion and protein pathology across diverse cell types.

top10_weekly.title: A chemomechanical bifurcation landscape unifies sustained growth, length homeostasis, and regenerative collapse in axons.
top10_weekly.abstract: Axonal growth machinery is largely shared across neurons, but axons exhibit strikingly different fates depending on developmental and environmental context: sustained elongation in peripheral neurons under permissive conditions, length homeostasis in cortical neurons after target innervation, and pathological collapse into dystrophic endbulbs in injured adult central nervous system (CNS) axons. These divergent outcomes have resisted explanation by length-sensing and biomechanical models that treat long-range transport and local force generation as separate problems. We unify these phenomena through a mechanochemical model that couples bidirectional motor transport and intracellular signaling to growth-cone balance of axonal tension, actomyosin contraction, and adhesion within a single feedback loop: The lengthening axon uses its own growing transport delay to establish self-limiting mechanical feedback, as the accumulating delay reshapes signaling waveforms to progressively elevate myosin contractility against actin-driven protrusion. Two physical parameters, the transport delay and the signaling feedback strength, organize axon fate into a unified state-space landscape spanning sustained growth, length homeostasis, and pathological collapse. Reduced feedback strength weakens this self-limiting mechanical feedback by simultaneously enhancing protrusion and suppressing contractility, providing a mechanistic interpretation of axon lengthening under partial reduction of retrograde transport. Bistability in the inhibitory regime explains why mature CNS tracts persist where nascent sprouts collapse, recasting regenerative failure as a state-dependent gate rather than a capacity limit. The framework predicts that partial rather than complete inhibition of retrograde transport could shift collapsed axons across the bifurcation into a growth-permissive regime, identifying a class of interventions complementary to existing capacity-restoration strategies for nerve injury.

top10_weekly.title: Cellular-resolution three-photon ultra-deep imaging (TrUDI) of neuronal population activity at 2-mm depth in the mammalian brain.
top10_weekly.abstract: Extending the depth reach of multiphoton microscopy for imaging neuronal population activity in the scattering mammalian brain is an 'exponentially hard' problem. Three-photon (3p) microscopy has enabled imaging of neuroactivity at depths up to ~1.2 mm in the mouse brain; however, the fundamental depth limit of 3p imaging, as set by the depth at which out-of-focus background fluorescence exceeds the in-focus fluorescence signal, is well beyond 2 mm. Reaching this fundamental depth limit in 3p imaging has been hampered by insufficient in-focus fluorescence signal. Here we demonstrate a three-photon ultra-deep imaging (TrUDI) system that approaches this fundamental depth limit via systematic and principled optimization of the in-focus fluorescence signal. TrUDI matches the parameters of the excitation laser, the optical system, and the acquisition to linear and nonlinear limits for safe laser exposure while satisfying the spatiotemporal requirements of single-cell resolution calcium (Ca2+) imaging. TrUDI achieves a ~250-fold increase in detected fluorescence photon yield at the same laser power as in previous approaches thereby enabling in vivo cellular-resolution recordings of neuronal population activity within fields of view of ~230 × 230 µm2 at 8.6 Hz at tissue depths of up to ~2 mm in mouse cortex and hippocampus.

top10_weekly.title: Lightweight Instance Segmentation Network for Microscopic Images of Suspension-Cultured B Cells Integrating Edge Priors and Multi-Scale Attention.
top10_weekly.abstract: Precise single-cell analysis is important for life sciences and precision medicine. In antibody drug discovery and immunotherapy, automated segmentation and quantitative analysis of suspension-cultured B cells in label-free bright-field microscopic images can support image-based characterization of cell populations under the recorded culture conditions. However, accurate segmentation remains challenging because of weak boundary gradients, heterogeneous cell sizes, background interference, and high-density clustering. Existing deep learning models may also face a trade-off between segmentation performance and model compactness, which can limit their use in resource-constrained automated microscopy systems. To address these challenges, we propose EPMSA-Net, a lightweight instance segmentation network that integrates edge priors and multi-scale attention for B-cell image analysis. The proposed framework incorporates two complementary structures: the Edge-Aware Feature Preservation (EAFP) module supplements weak boundary-related and local spatial cues during early feature extraction, whereas the Multi-Scale Contextual Attention (MSCA) module subsequently models multi-scale contextual information and recalibrates downstream feature responses. Evaluation on the current suspension-cultured B-cell dataset yielded an F1-score of 94.44% ± 0.53% and an Aggregated Jaccard Index (AJI) of 89.87% ± 0.78% over five independent training runs, with a parameter count of 3.276 M. Density-stratified evaluation showed relatively small F1-score variation across the predefined low-, medium-, and high-density subsets, with a mean CVF1 of 0.84% ± 0.13%. The resulting instance masks were further used to calculate image-level cell count and segmented area ratio (SAR). These results indicate that EPMSA-Net achieves competitive segmentation performance with a compact model size on the current dataset. Further validation across independent culture batches, imaging systems, and hardware platforms is required to evaluate its broader applicability and deployment performance.

primary.title: Insights into how JIP3 and JIP4 adaptor proteins relieve the auto-inhibited form of the kinesin-1 motor.
primary.abstract: While our understanding of kinesin autoinhibition mechanisms is advancing, key insights into kinesin activation, especially autoinhibition relieved by cargo-motor adaptors, remain unclear. JIP3 and JIP4 are adaptors that activate kinesin-1 and dynein-dynactin motors, enabling bidirectional transport along microtubules. Here, we characterized the interaction between the kinesin-1 heavy chain, KIF5B, and both JIP3 and JIP4 (JIP3/4), using mutagenesis and binding experiments associated with modelling. We identified the minimal regions of JIP3/4 and KIF5B required for interaction. JIP3/4 binds to the CC4 coiled-coil domain of KIF5B, with no significant interaction detected with the distal tail. Conversely, KIF5B-CC4 binds to the RH1 domain of JIP3/4, with the preceding disordered N-terminus modulating the force of the binding. Notably, JIP3 and JIP4 exhibit ∼40-fold differences in affinity for KIF5B. We performed extensive site-directed mutagenesis on KIF5B-binding regions of JIP3/JIP4 targeting accessible charged residues and sequence differences between JIP3 and JIP4. This revealed multiple weak-affinity binding sites that collectively define an extensive KIF5B-binding surface on the RH1 domain of JIP3. Importantly, the KIF5B-binding surface on JIP3 differs from that of the DLIC (dynein light intermediate chain), confirming no competition between the two motors. Altogether, the fragment and mutant mapping of KIF5B binding to JIP3 and JIP4 presented here provides insights into how the auto-inhibited form of kinesin-1 might be relieved, with the CC4 region playing a central role.

primary.title: Ultrastructural studies reveal a new role for JIP3/MAPK8IP3 in endo-lysosomal maturation within the neuronal cell body.
primary.abstract: In recent years, substantial heterogeneity in lysosomes, in terms of their composition, function, and positioning, has come to be recognized. Despite this, there are gaps in knowledge of our understanding of the molecular basis of lysosome heterogeneity, especially in neurons. To this end, we used electron microscopy to define endolysosomal organelles of human iPSC-derived neurons at the ultrastructural level. Through this, we identify endolysosomal maturation defects within neuronal cell bodies of iNeurons lacking JNK-Interacting Protein 3 (JIP3), a lysosome adaptor previously known to primarily regulate axonal lysosome movement. Loss of JIP3 results in an expansion of immature lysosomes within neuronal soma, along with a concomitant decrease in mature lysosomes. JIP3 loss also leads to delayed trafficking of endocytic cargo through these compartments, implicating JIP3 in the regulation of endolysosomal maturation within neuronal cell bodies. Our studies highlight the utility of electron microscopy in understanding neuronal lysosomal heterogeneity. Additionally, given recent links between JIP3 and a neurodevelopmental disorder, our findings here could provide new insight into mechanisms underlying neurodevelopmental pathology.

primary.title: JIP4 and RILPL1 utilize opposing motor force to dynamically regulate lysosomal tubulation.
primary.abstract: Lysosomes are dynamic organelles that remodel their membrane in response to stimuli. We previously uncovered a process we term LYsosomal Tubulation/sorting driven by LRRK2 (LYTL), wherein damaged lysosomes generate tubules sorted into vesicles. LYTL is orchestrated by the Parkinson's disease kinase LRRK2 that recruits the motor adaptor protein and RHD family member JIP4 to lysosomes. JIP4 enhances LYTL tubule extension toward the plus-end of microtubules. To identify new players involved in LYTL, we mapped the lysosomal proteome after LRRK2 kinase inhibition. We found that RILPL1 is recruited to dysfunctional lysosomes in an LRRK2 kinase activity-dependent manner, facilitated by pRAB proteins. Unlike JIP4, RILPL1 induces retraction of LYTL tubules by binding to p150Glued, thereby moving lysosomal tubules toward the minus-end of microtubules. Our findings emphasize the dynamic regulation of LYTL tubules by two distinct RHD proteins and pRAB effectors, acting as opposing motor adaptor proteins. These opposing forces create a metastable lysosomal membrane deformation, enabling dynamic tubulation events.

primary.title: Disruption of dynactin complex function in intellectual disability.
primary.abstract: Intellectual disability (ID) is a highly prevalent condition affecting approximately 200 millions of people worldwide, characterized by impaired cognitive function. Dynactin complex consists of multiple protein subunits and is required for intracellular trafficking and synaptic homeostasis in developing and mature neurons. Here, we identify deleterious variants of dynactin subunit 4 (DCTN4) in ID pedigrees. DCTN4 ablation in mice results in altered neuronal positioning and apoptosis in neural progenitor cells. Notably, mice carrying the ID-linked DCTN4 variant exhibit cognitive deficits with impaired dendritic development. Cortical neurons with DCTN4 deficiency or variant show reduced levels of various dynactin subunits, suggesting that deficits in dynactin complex affects synaptic function. Furthermore, disruption of the DCTN4-JIP3 complex impairs lysosomal transport and dendritic development as well as synaptic development. Importantly, we showed that damaging variants in another dynactin subunit DCTN2 also disrupt neuronal positioning, reinforcing the critical role of dynactin complex in neurodevelopment and ID pathogenesis. These findings illustrate dysfunctional dynactin complex as a previously unrecognized disease mechanism of ID.

secondary.title: Characterization of a novel inherited splice-site variant in MAPK8IP3 expands the genetic and phenotypic spectrum of neurodevelopmental disorders.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: The MAPK8IP3 gene encodes JIP3, a kinesin-1 adapter protein crucial for axonal transport and JNK signaling pathway regulation. This gene exhibits extreme intolerance to loss-of-function variants. Heterozygous pathogenic MAPK8IP3 variants are linked to a neurodevelopmental disorder with or without variable brain abnormalities (NEDBA). This study characterizes a novel inherited canonical splice-site variant identified in a three-generation family. METHODS: Exome sequencing was performed on three affected individuals from a single non-consanguineous family with presenting neurological abnormalities. The molecular consequences of the identified variant were evaluated by RNA analysis. Clinical features of the variant carriers were evaluated in detail. RESULTS: We identified a heterozygous dinucleotide deletion (c.2630-2_2630-1del) at the canonical acceptor splice site of MAPK8IP3. This variant co-segregated with the neurological phenotype in an affected mother and her two children. RNA analysis demonstrated that this variant leads to a partial deletion of exon 22 (r.2630_2673del), which is predicted to cause a frameshift and introduce a premature termination codon (p.Gly877Valfs∗36). Notably, despite carrying an identical genotype, the three affected individuals exhibited marked interindividual variability in clinical severity, ranging from mild specific learning difficulties to global developmental delay with severe intellectual disability and autism. CONCLUSION: This represents the first report of a familial, autosomal dominantly inherited pathogenic splice-site variant in MAPK8IP3, extending the established inheritance pattern beyond previously described de novo events. Our findings expand both the mutational and phenotypic spectrum of MAPK8IP3-related disorders, highlighting the complexity of genotype-phenotype correlations and underscoring the necessity of functional assays for accurate variant interpretation.

best.title: Insights into how JIP3 and JIP4 adaptor proteins relieve the auto-inhibited form of the kinesin-1 motor.
best.abstract: While our understanding of kinesin autoinhibition mechanisms is advancing, key insights into kinesin activation, especially autoinhibition relieved by cargo-motor adaptors, remain unclear. JIP3 and JIP4 are adaptors that activate kinesin-1 and dynein-dynactin motors, enabling bidirectional transport along microtubules. Here, we characterized the interaction between the kinesin-1 heavy chain, KIF5B, and both JIP3 and JIP4 (JIP3/4), using mutagenesis and binding experiments associated with modelling. We identified the minimal regions of JIP3/4 and KIF5B required for interaction. JIP3/4 binds to the CC4 coiled-coil domain of KIF5B, with no significant interaction detected with the distal tail. Conversely, KIF5B-CC4 binds to the RH1 domain of JIP3/4, with the preceding disordered N-terminus modulating the force of the binding. Notably, JIP3 and JIP4 exhibit ∼40-fold differences in affinity for KIF5B. We performed extensive site-directed mutagenesis on KIF5B-binding regions of JIP3/JIP4 targeting accessible charged residues and sequence differences between JIP3 and JIP4. This revealed multiple weak-affinity binding sites that collectively define an extensive KIF5B-binding surface on the RH1 domain of JIP3. Importantly, the KIF5B-binding surface on JIP3 differs from that of the DLIC (dynein light intermediate chain), confirming no competition between the two motors. Altogether, the fragment and mutant mapping of KIF5B binding to JIP3 and JIP4 presented here provides insights into how the auto-inhibited form of kinesin-1 might be relieved, with the CC4 region playing a central role.

best.title: Ultrastructural studies reveal a new role for JIP3/MAPK8IP3 in endo-lysosomal maturation within the neuronal cell body.
best.abstract: In recent years, substantial heterogeneity in lysosomes, in terms of their composition, function, and positioning, has come to be recognized. Despite this, there are gaps in knowledge of our understanding of the molecular basis of lysosome heterogeneity, especially in neurons. To this end, we used electron microscopy to define endolysosomal organelles of human iPSC-derived neurons at the ultrastructural level. Through this, we identify endolysosomal maturation defects within neuronal cell bodies of iNeurons lacking JNK-Interacting Protein 3 (JIP3), a lysosome adaptor previously known to primarily regulate axonal lysosome movement. Loss of JIP3 results in an expansion of immature lysosomes within neuronal soma, along with a concomitant decrease in mature lysosomes. JIP3 loss also leads to delayed trafficking of endocytic cargo through these compartments, implicating JIP3 in the regulation of endolysosomal maturation within neuronal cell bodies. Our studies highlight the utility of electron microscopy in understanding neuronal lysosomal heterogeneity. Additionally, given recent links between JIP3 and a neurodevelopmental disorder, our findings here could provide new insight into mechanisms underlying neurodevelopmental pathology.

best.title: Characterization of a novel inherited splice-site variant in MAPK8IP3 expands the genetic and phenotypic spectrum of neurodevelopmental disorders.
best.abstract: BACKGROUND: The MAPK8IP3 gene encodes JIP3, a kinesin-1 adapter protein crucial for axonal transport and JNK signaling pathway regulation. This gene exhibits extreme intolerance to loss-of-function variants. Heterozygous pathogenic MAPK8IP3 variants are linked to a neurodevelopmental disorder with or without variable brain abnormalities (NEDBA). This study characterizes a novel inherited canonical splice-site variant identified in a three-generation family. METHODS: Exome sequencing was performed on three affected individuals from a single non-consanguineous family with presenting neurological abnormalities. The molecular consequences of the identified variant were evaluated by RNA analysis. Clinical features of the variant carriers were evaluated in detail. RESULTS: We identified a heterozygous dinucleotide deletion (c.2630-2_2630-1del) at the canonical acceptor splice site of MAPK8IP3. This variant co-segregated with the neurological phenotype in an affected mother and her two children. RNA analysis demonstrated that this variant leads to a partial deletion of exon 22 (r.2630_2673del), which is predicted to cause a frameshift and introduce a premature termination codon (p.Gly877Valfs∗36). Notably, despite carrying an identical genotype, the three affected individuals exhibited marked interindividual variability in clinical severity, ranging from mild specific learning difficulties to global developmental delay with severe intellectual disability and autism. CONCLUSION: This represents the first report of a familial, autosomal dominantly inherited pathogenic splice-site variant in MAPK8IP3, extending the established inheritance pattern beyond previously described de novo events. Our findings expand both the mutational and phenotypic spectrum of MAPK8IP3-related disorders, highlighting the complexity of genotype-phenotype correlations and underscoring the necessity of functional assays for accurate variant interpretation.

best.title: JIP4 and RILPL1 utilize opposing motor force to dynamically regulate lysosomal tubulation.
best.abstract: Lysosomes are dynamic organelles that remodel their membrane in response to stimuli. We previously uncovered a process we term LYsosomal Tubulation/sorting driven by LRRK2 (LYTL), wherein damaged lysosomes generate tubules sorted into vesicles. LYTL is orchestrated by the Parkinson's disease kinase LRRK2 that recruits the motor adaptor protein and RHD family member JIP4 to lysosomes. JIP4 enhances LYTL tubule extension toward the plus-end of microtubules. To identify new players involved in LYTL, we mapped the lysosomal proteome after LRRK2 kinase inhibition. We found that RILPL1 is recruited to dysfunctional lysosomes in an LRRK2 kinase activity-dependent manner, facilitated by pRAB proteins. Unlike JIP4, RILPL1 induces retraction of LYTL tubules by binding to p150Glued, thereby moving lysosomal tubules toward the minus-end of microtubules. Our findings emphasize the dynamic regulation of LYTL tubules by two distinct RHD proteins and pRAB effectors, acting as opposing motor adaptor proteins. These opposing forces create a metastable lysosomal membrane deformation, enabling dynamic tubulation events.

best.title: Disruption of dynactin complex function in intellectual disability.
best.abstract: Intellectual disability (ID) is a highly prevalent condition affecting approximately 200 millions of people worldwide, characterized by impaired cognitive function. Dynactin complex consists of multiple protein subunits and is required for intracellular trafficking and synaptic homeostasis in developing and mature neurons. Here, we identify deleterious variants of dynactin subunit 4 (DCTN4) in ID pedigrees. DCTN4 ablation in mice results in altered neuronal positioning and apoptosis in neural progenitor cells. Notably, mice carrying the ID-linked DCTN4 variant exhibit cognitive deficits with impaired dendritic development. Cortical neurons with DCTN4 deficiency or variant show reduced levels of various dynactin subunits, suggesting that deficits in dynactin complex affects synaptic function. Furthermore, disruption of the DCTN4-JIP3 complex impairs lysosomal transport and dendritic development as well as synaptic development. Importantly, we showed that damaging variants in another dynactin subunit DCTN2 also disrupt neuronal positioning, reinforcing the critical role of dynactin complex in neurodevelopment and ID pathogenesis. These findings illustrate dysfunctional dynactin complex as a previously unrecognized disease mechanism of ID.

primary.title: KCNH1 variants associated with neurodevelopmental disorders exhibit prominent gain of function.
primary.abstract: Pathogenic variants in KCNH1, encoding the human ether-á-go-go voltage-gated potassium channel (EAG1, KV10.1), are associated with the neurodevelopmental disorders Temple-Baraitser syndrome (TBS), Zimmermann-Laband syndrome (ZLS), epileptic encephalopathy, and other undefined neurodevelopmental disorders. Investigating the functional consequences of KCNH1 variants can provide information about molecular and cellular pathophysiological mechanisms and help guide therapeutic directions. In this study, we determined the functional properties of 26 disease-associated KCNH1 variants including three recurrent and six that were previously unpublished. Findings were compared to the wildtype (WT) channel along with six rare population variants. Our approach used automated patch clamp recording of heterologously expressed KCNH1 variants in both the homozygous state (variant alone) and the clinically-relevant heterozygous state (variant co-expressed with WT channels). We also examined the impact of alternative splice isoforms on functional consequences of specific variants. We demonstrated that the majority of disease-associated KCNH1 variants exhibit features consistent with gain-of-function including hyperpolarized voltage-dependence of activation, accelerated activation kinetics, or both that promote hyperpolarization of the resting membrane potential. By contrast, one unique variant discovered previously in an autism cohort had a depolarized voltage-dependence of activation and was associated with a depolarized resting potential in cells. Pharmacological testing of KCNH1 variants demonstrated differences in potency for channel block by imipramine and an investigational non-selective potassium channel blocker (LY97241) for specific variants. Collectively, our findings support gain-of-function as the most common, albeit not exclusive, molecular mechanism underlying KCNH1-related disorders and suggest opportunities for potential therapeutic drug repurposing strategies for these conditions.

primary.title: Altered stability of dynamic functional architecture in the co-occurrence of autism spectrum disorder and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder.
primary.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) frequently co-occur, whereas the underlying neurobiological mechanisms remain largely unexplored. This study aimed to identify alterations in dynamic functional architecture across ASD, ADHD, and their comorbidity. This study selected 287 participants from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange and ADHD-200 datasets, divided into ASD without ADHD (ASD-only), ADHD without ASD (ADHD-only), ASD + ADHD, and typically developing (TD) groups. In this study, we employed dynamic functional stability at the voxel level by measuring the temporal concordance of dynamic functional connectivity (DFC). Furthermore, whole-brain DFC analyses were conducted using clusters with significant stability alterations as seed regions. Group comparisons and correlation analyses were subsequently performed. Our results showed significant group differences in functional stability in the left superior frontal gyrus, orbital part (ORBsup), right pallidum, and left amygdala. Seed-based analyses identified altered DFC variability between the left amygdala and three regions, including the right middle temporal gyrus (MTG), the left insula, and the left superior occipital gyrus (SOG). Notably, DFC variability between the left amygdala and right MTG was significantly negatively correlated with Social Communication Questionnaire (SCQ) scores in the comorbidity group (r = - 0.620, p < 0.01, FDR corrected). From a dynamic perspective, our findings revealed that ASD, ADHD, and their comorbidity exhibited commonanduniquechanges in brain function, thereby enhancing our understanding of the pathogenesis underlying ASD + ADHD.

primary.title: Maternal edible THC consumption alters offspring neurodevelopment and emotional behavior in rhesus macaques.
primary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Prenatal cannabis exposure is associated with adverse offspring outcomes including altered neurodevelopment. However, there is insufficient evidence to establish a direct association. We sought to determine the impact of chronic prenatal delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) exposure on offspring neurodevelopment and emotional behavior in a translational rhesus macaque model. METHODS: Animals were divided into two groups, control and THC-exposed, with both groups receiving a daily edible (placebo or THC) pre-conception, throughout pregnancy, and postnatally. MRI was performed longitudinally across gestation and infancy to assess volumetric and microstructural brain development. Serial behavioral testing, including motor and emotional assessments, was performed postnatally. At 6 months of age, brain tissue was collected for histology, immunohistochemistry (IHC), whole genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS), and bulk RNA-sequencing. FINDINGS: Analysis of the MRI images showed white matter changes with higher fractional anisotropy in the corpus callosum (CC) and centrum semiovale in THC-exposed infants. However, there were no significant differences in regional brain volumes. Behavioral testing demonstrated that THC-exposed infants displayed increased vocalizations and decreased independence. WGBS identified differentially methylated regions (DMRs) associated with THC exposure in the cerebellum and prefrontal cortex, annotated to genes involved in synaptic organization and brain development. RNA-sequencing confirmed differential expression of genes related to axon development and glutamatergic synapse, with expression correlating with methylation levels. INTERPRETATION: Chronic prenatal edible THC exposure in the rhesus macaque was associated with changes in white matter development, effects on infant behavior with signs of increased stress and anxiety, and brain DNA methylation and expression of genes involved in neurodevelopment. primary.title: Domain-associated phenotypic patterns with MACF1 variants.
primary.abstract: PURPOSE: While heterozygous de novo missense variants in the microtubule-binding GAR domain of Microtubule-actin cross-linking factor 1 (MACF1) cause Lissencephaly 9 with Complex Brainstem Malformations (LIS9) [MIM 618325], the phenotypic impact of variants outside this domain remains unclear. METHODS: We assembled a cohort of 5 affected individuals from 4 unrelated families with biallelic non-GAR domain MACF1 variants who exhibit partially overlapping yet unique phenotypic traits. A sixth individual with a de novo, heterozygous frameshift variant was additionally identified. Combined with previously reported cases, we analyzed genotype and phenotype data from 22 individuals using Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO)-based unsupervised hierarchical clustering. RESULTS: Clustering revealed two distinct phenotypic signatures, suggesting domain-associated effects. Variants outside the GAR domain associate with broader neurodevelopmental phenotypes and craniofacial and skeletal involvement. Enrichment analysis (p < 0.001) using OMIM HPO sets supported these findings. In contrast to the GAR domain's strong correlation with LIS9, biallelic non-GAR domain MACF1 variants were linked to distinct developmental anomalies. CONCLUSION: These results expand the phenotypic spectrum of MACF1-related disorders and provide preliminary evidence for domain-associated MACF1 variant effects. While limited by sample size and lack of functional validation, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and underscore the utility of HPO-based clustering for systematic phenotype comparison as additional cases emerge. Comprehensive genetic and phenotypic assessments are essential for understanding the role of MACF1 in development, informing diagnosis, and guiding future research on cytoskeletal regulation in neurodevelopment.

primary.title: Altered medial prefrontal-striatal connectivity and plasticity in humanized CBLN2 mice.
primary.abstract: Deciphering processes that are responsible for differences in brain development and architecture among species may provide clues to the species-specific program and may facilitate a mechanistic understanding of vulnerability to neuropsychiatric disorders. It has recently been shown that the promoter of the CBLN2 gene, which codes for a synaptogenic factor, cerebellin 2 (Cbln2), has a repressor element in mice but not in humans. A humanized mouse lacking this repressor (hCbln2) reproduces higher spine density in medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) neurons and higher corticothalamic connectivity observed in humans. Cbln2 is part of a trans-synaptic complex that includes glutamate delta-1 receptor (GluD1) and neurexins (Nrxn) (GluD1-Cbln2-Nrxn). Interestingly, we have previously reported a contrasting striatal patch-matrix expression pattern of GluD1 in mouse versus monkey, suggesting a potential role of the GluD1-Cbln complex in species differences. In this study, we examined the synaptic organization and function in the cortex and dorsal striatum of hCbln2 mice. Consistent with previous reports, hCbln2 mice exhibited increased vGluT1 expression in the mPFC, indicating enhanced intracortical connectivity. Electrophysiological recordings further revealed an increased mEPSC frequency along with a reduced mIPSC frequency in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons, suggesting an increase in excitatory/inhibitory balance. These changes were accompanied by enhanced mTOR signalling and autophagic deficits in the mPFC. Contrasting synaptic changes were observed in the striatum with an increase in vGluT2 and a reduction in vGluT1, together with a decrease in GluD1-Cbln1 and an increase in hevin. Importantly, corticostriatal dysfunction characterized by a reduction in cortical contribution to mEPSCs and impaired DHPG-induced synaptic depression was observed in the hCbln2 medium spiny neurons. Further, hCbln2 mice displayed increased repetitive behaviour together with social and affective-like deficits, consistent with autism-relevant phenotypes. Collectively, these findings identify humanized Cbln2 regulation as a driver of divergent cortical and striatal synaptic remodelling, disrupted corticostriatal synaptic function, and behavioural abnormalities relevant to neurodevelopmental disorders.

primary.title: Overexpression of endoplasmic reticulum acetyl-CoA transporter AT-1 alters neuronal metabolism, growth, and synaptic activity.
primary.abstract: Acetyl-CoA is a molecule central to cellular metabolic homeostasis. As part of the secretory pathway, acetyl-CoA is imported into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by a membrane-bound transporter AT-1 (SLC33A1). AT-1 mutations have been linked to peripheral neuropathy, developmental delay with premature death, and intellectual disability with progeria. Here, we show that AT-1 overexpression impacts diverse phenotypes related to neuronal function and plasticity. Differences in ribosomal, synaptic processing, and metabolic pathways were identified at transcriptomic and proteomic levels. Metabolic adaptations included changes in mitochondrial membrane potential, architecture, and respiration, and tracing experiments revealed changes in the fate of glucose favoring glycogen storage over the pentose phosphate pathway. Altered redox was linked to NAD-dependent proteins SIRT1 and CtBP2. Depletion of lipid stores was associated with greater plasticity in fuel substrate utilization. Metabolic adaptation was coincident with decreased synaptic activity, indicating that neuronal communication is coordinated, in part, through acetyl-CoA metabolism.

primary.title: Disruption of dynactin complex function in intellectual disability.
primary.abstract: Intellectual disability (ID) is a highly prevalent condition affecting approximately 200 millions of people worldwide, characterized by impaired cognitive function. Dynactin complex consists of multiple protein subunits and is required for intracellular trafficking and synaptic homeostasis in developing and mature neurons. Here, we identify deleterious variants of dynactin subunit 4 (DCTN4) in ID pedigrees. DCTN4 ablation in mice results in altered neuronal positioning and apoptosis in neural progenitor cells. Notably, mice carrying the ID-linked DCTN4 variant exhibit cognitive deficits with impaired dendritic development. Cortical neurons with DCTN4 deficiency or variant show reduced levels of various dynactin subunits, suggesting that deficits in dynactin complex affects synaptic function. Furthermore, disruption of the DCTN4-JIP3 complex impairs lysosomal transport and dendritic development as well as synaptic development. Importantly, we showed that damaging variants in another dynactin subunit DCTN2 also disrupt neuronal positioning, reinforcing the critical role of dynactin complex in neurodevelopment and ID pathogenesis. These findings illustrate dysfunctional dynactin complex as a previously unrecognized disease mechanism of ID.

secondary.title: Neonatal-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy: High genetic yield and long-term outcomes in a multicenter southern European cohort.
secondary.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To determine the genetic diagnostic yield, characterize the clinical and genetic landscape, and evaluate long-term epilepsy, neurodevelopmental, and survival outcomes in a strictly defined cohort of neonatal-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE). METHODS: Retrospective multicenter observational study across tertiary epilepsy centers in Italy, Greece, and Spain. Sixty-two full-term neonates fulfilling ILAE 2022 criteria for DEE with seizure onset within the first 30 days of life and a minimum follow-up of 18 months were included. All patients underwent next-generation sequencing-based genetic testing. Genetic findings, clinical characteristics, and long-term outcomes were systematically analyzed. RESULTS: A molecular diagnosis was established in 82.2% of patients (51/62), identifying variants across 29 genes grouped, for descriptive purposes, into four broad categories according to principal biological role. First-line whole-exome sequencing achieved higher diagnostic yield than targeted gene panels (88.9% vs. 41.2%), although this comparison was influenced by differences in testing era and strategy. KCNQ2 variants were the most frequent genetic cause (29.4%), and several treatable metabolic disorders were identified. After a mean follow-up of 11.9 years, 64.5% of patients had drug-resistant epilepsy and mortality reached 17.7%. Seizure freedom was achieved in a subset of patients, particularly those with KCNQ2-related DEE. Nevertheless, severe-to-profound intellectual disability affected 71.7% of evaluable patients and persisted even among those who became seizure-free, suggesting that neurodevelopmental outcomes are influenced by factors beyond seizure burden, including the underlying genetic disorder and other disease-related factors. However, the marked variability observed precludes any causal inference from these data. SIGNIFICANCE: This large European cohort demonstrates a high genetic diagnostic yield in neonatal-onset DEE, supporting first-line whole-exome sequencing as the preferred first-tier genetic test. The persistence of severe neurodevelopmental impairment despite seizure control highlights the need for precision therapies targeting disease mechanisms in addition to seizure management. PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: We studied 62 newborns who developed severe epilepsy caused by genetic changes, following them for up to 25 years. We found a genetic cause in over 80% of cases, and genetic testing that reads the entire genetic code was far more effective than tests that only look at specific genes. Although seizures improved in some children over time, nearly all had lasting intellectual disability regardless of seizure control. This suggests that the underlying genetic condition may contribute substantially to brain development in addition to the effects of seizures, although our study cannot determine the relative contribution of each factor.

secondary.title: Striatofugal balance and beneficial effects of facilitating nucleus accumbens mGlu4 receptor activity in the Fmr1-/- mouse model of Fragile X Syndrome.
secondary.abstract: Fragile X Syndrome (FXS) is the leading monogenic cause of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). To date, no approved pharmacological treatment alleviates social impairments in patients with FXS. Since D1 and D2 dopamine receptor-expressing striatal projection neurons (SPNs) were shown to regulate ASD-sensitive behaviors, we explored whether the balance of activity between D1- and D2-SPNs would be biased in the Fmr1-/- mouse model of FXS. We evaluated striatal function in Fmr1-/- and Fmr1+/+ mice under pharmacological challenge and performed RNAscope® in situ hybridization following social interaction to assess the activity of SPNs in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and dorsal striatum. We evidenced a decrease in D1-SPN activity, biasing the D1/D2-SPN balance. We then evaluated the effects of compounds developed to repress D2-SPN activity on behavioral impairments in Fmr1-/- mice. Systemically facilitating mGlu4 or blocking A2a receptor activity relieved behavioral deficits in this model. Moreover, social interaction in Fmr1-/- mice was fully rescued by photopharmacological activation of mGlu4 in the ventral pallidum, to which both NAc D1- and D2-SPNs project, and mGlu4 receptors in the NAc likely contributed to restoring social deficits after systemic mGlu4 facilitation. Together, these results are consistent with our working hypotheses of both biased striatal D1/D2-SPN balance in social deficit and contribution of mGlu4 receptors expressed by NAc SPNs in modulating social behavior. In conclusion, pharmacological compounds able to regulate SPN activity demonstrate a promising therapeutic potential to relieve ASD-like deficits in FXS. secondary.title: CNTN4: A Possible Candidate Gene for Microbiota-Gut-Brain Axis in Autism Spectrum Disorders and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder.
secondary.abstract: The gut microbiota plays a significant role in autism spectrum disorders (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), though findings vary substantially across studies. Using gut microbiome data from a genome-wide association study of 5,959 participants and summary statistics from 46,351 ASD and 55,374 ADHD cases, we conducted bidirectional Mendelian randomization (MR) analyses with inverse variance weighting as the primary method. Reverse MR analysis assessed potential reverse causality. We annotated single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) with SNP-nexus to identify associated genes, followed by Gene Ontology (﻿GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses to characterize their functional roles. Seventeen gut microbial taxa showed causal associations with ASD risk, while 27 were linked to ADHD. Reverse MR analysis revealed associations between aSD and species Desulfovibrio piger as well as species Bacillus U, but no reverse causality was detected for ADHD. Biological annotation identified five novel conserved genes in host-microbiome interactions shared by ASD and ADHD, with CNTN4 emerging as a common candidate gene. These findings support a potential causal relationship between gut microbiota and ASD/ADHD risk while uncovering novel conserved genes implicated in host-microbiome interactions for both disorders.Lay AbstractDistinct gut microbiota profiles were observed in individuals with ADHD and ASD. Seventeen microbial species showed significant associations with ASD, while 27 were linked to ADHD. CNTN4 emerged as a potential candidate gene shared across both neurodevelopmental conditions and host-microbiome interactions.

secondary.title: Recurrent Neurodevelopmental Disorder Associated With a Dominant-Negative TOP2B H63Y Variant.
secondary.abstract: We describe a 7 year-old boy with severe neurodevelopmental disorder, medically-refractory epileptic encephalopathy, hyperkinetic movement disorder, hypotonia, cerebral and cerebellar atrophy and hypomyelination who was found to have a heterozygous de novo TOP2B NM_001330700.2:c.187C>T, p.(His63Tyr) variant. This is the third individual reported with the H63Y variant and severe neurodevelopmental disorder. The phenotype associated with the H63Y variant differs greatly from the TOP2B-related Immunodeficiency and Congenital Anomalies Spectrum (TICAS) syndrome that has been reported with heterozygous loss-of-function variants affecting the TOPRIM domain and adjacent regions of TOP2B. DNA topoisomerase II beta (TOP2B) is an essential enzyme that resolves DNA supercoils and knots to facilitate transcription and replication. To investigate the functional impact of this variant, we studied the homologous yeast variant, top2 H20Y (H20Y). Homozygous H20Y strains exhibited reduced viability, while heterozygous H20Y acted as a loss-of-function allele incapable of supporting growth. Overexpression of the chimeric human H63Y variant in yeast was lethal. Despite its dysfunction, H63Y retains partial enzymatic activity and appears to function as a dominant negative variant that induces DNA damage. Thus, this work establishes a novel gene-disease association between TOP2B-H63Y and a neurodevelopmental disorder we propose to name TOP2B-related neurodevelopmental disorder. Further studies should elucidate the pathogenic mechanisms underlying H63Y-associated phenotypes.

secondary.title: WWOX-related developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (WOREE): A case series of seven patients from Argentina.
secondary.abstract: PURPOSE: WWOX-related developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (WOREE) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic WWOX variants, characterized by very early-onset epilepsy, profound developmental delay, and progressive brain abnormalities. Detailed electroclinical descriptions remain limited. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective study of seven patients with pathogenic/likely pathogenic WWOX variants. Clinical features, seizure evolution, EEG findings, brain MRI, and genetic data were reviewed. Epilepsy syndromes were classified according to International League against Epilepsy (ILAE) criteria. Variants were identified through next-generation sequencing and interpreted following American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) guidelines. RESULTS: Median seizure onset was 3 months (range 2-6). Five patients presented with focal seizures evolving to infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (IESS), while two had IESS at onset. Epilepsy was drug-resistant in all. Developmental delay was evident from birth with generalized hypotonia, acquired microcephaly, and impaired visual attention. Four patients had dysmorphic features. During the IESS period, EEG showed hypsarrhythmia in six patients and a severely disorganized encephalopathic background that did not strictly fulfill the criteria for hypsarrhythmia in one. Brain MRI revealed abnormalities in all patients, including frontotemporal atrophy and corpus callosum hypoplasia; delayed myelination was observed in one case. Eight pathogenic/likely pathogenic WWOX variants were found; including one novel variant (NM_016373.4:c.571C>T, p.(Gln191*)). The recurrent splice-site variant NM_016373.4:c.107+1G>A was identified in five patients, suggesting a possible regional founder effect. CONCLUSION: WOREE shows a recognizable electroclinical and neuroimaging profile with early drug-resistant epilepsy and profound developmental delay. Recognition of this pattern may facilitate early diagnosis and targeted genetic testing, particularly in populations with recurrent variants.

secondary.title: Deep brain stimulation of the nucleus basalis magnocellularis ameliorates autistic behavior in a rat model of autism via cholinergic modulation in the prefrontal cortex.
secondary.abstract: OBJECTIVE: In the present study, we investigated whether deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the nucleus basalis magnocellularis (NBM) improves autism spectrum disorder (ASD)-related behavioral abnormalities in a valproic acid (VPA)-induced rat model of autism, consistent with changes in cholinergic markers in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). METHODS: On the 12.5th day of gestation, pregnant rats ( n  = 16) received a single intraperitoneal injection of 500 mg/kg sodium valproate dissolved in 0.9% saline, while others ( n  = 5) received saline alone. Male offspring were allowed to reach 3 months of age and then were randomly assigned to one of four experimental groups: Contr - prenatally saline injected, VPA - prenatally VPA-injected, VPA/I - VPA-injected with electrode implantation in the NBM, and VPA/S - VPA-injected with electrical stimulation. DBS was initiated in rats of the VPA/S group 10 days after surgery (two consecutive hours per day, every day for 2 weeks; DBS parameters: 60 Hz, 120 µs, and 50 µA). RESULTS: The prenatally VPA-exposed rats demonstrate deficits in social behavior, increased locomotor activity, and reduced anxiety levels. Immunohistochemical evaluation shows a decrease in the number of acetylcholinesterase-immunoreactive neurons in the mPFC and choline acetyltransferase-immunoreactive neurons in the NBM. NBM-DBS improves VPA-induced autistic behavior and increases the number of acetylcholinesterase-immunoreactive neurons in the PFC. CONCLUSION: The correlation between ASD-like behavior and cholinergic markers in the mPFC supports our hypothesis that NBM-DBS improves behavioral deficits by modulating cholinergic neurotransmission in the PFC in a rat model of autism.

secondary.title: Biallelic SLC20A2 loss-of-function in severe early-onset neurodevelopmental disorder with brain calcification.
secondary.abstract: Biallelic SLC20A2 variants have recently been linked to a severe childhood-onset phenotype distinct from classical adult-onset primary brain calcification, but the molecular and radiologic consequences of homozygous truncating variants remain incompletely defined. We describe a child with severe early-onset neurodevelopmental disease caused by a homozygous SLC20A2 nonsense variant and provide clinical, neuroradiologic, segregation, and transcript-level characterization. The patient presented in early infancy with refractory seizures, severe hypotonia, left hemiplegia, profound developmental impairment, bilateral cataracts, and progressive intracranial calcification. Neuroimaging showed an unusual vascular and leptomeningeal calcification pattern with arterial narrowing, cytotoxic edema, subdural effusion, and rapid cerebral atrophy. Whole-exome sequencing identified a homozygous truncating variant, NM_001257180.2:c.1652 G > A, p.(Trp551Ter), in SLC20A2; both parents were heterozygous and showed radiologic findings consistent with SLC20A2-related primary brain calcification. RNA sequencing and RT-qPCR demonstrated marked reduction of SLC20A2 expression in patient-derived fibroblasts, supporting biallelic loss of function, whereas XPR1 expression was not significantly altered. Patient fibroblasts did not show overt Golgi fragmentation or ciliogenesis defects. These findings support a dose-dependent SLC20A2 disease spectrum and expand the phenotype associated with biallelic loss of function from primary brain calcification toward severe early-onset neurodevelopmental disorder with prominent vascular and leptomeningeal calcification.

secondary.title: Increased inflammatory cytokines in the temporal cortex in autism spectrum disorder.
secondary.abstract: Alterations in immune and neuroinflammatory processes are evident in neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism spectrum disorders (ASD). While prior studies using cerebrospinal fluid and plasma/serum have identified differences in cytokine levels in ASD when compared with controls, specific changes in postmortem human brain tissue remains poorly characterized. The superior temporal gyrus (STG) is involved in social communication and sensory processing, and is affected in ASD, making it a relevant region for investigating immune-related differences that has not been previously studied. Neuroimmune profiles were measured in STG tissue from 46 postmortem cases: ASD (n = 17), and neurotypical controls (n = 29). Fresh-frozen samples were collected using biopsy punches, and cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors were quantified using multiplexed bead immunoassays. In ASD cases, there were significantly increased levels of inflammatory cytokines in IL-1α, IL-8, IL-18, FLT-3L, FGF-2, G-CSF, M-CSF, MCP3, PDGF-AA and GROa compared to controls. In contrast, there was a significant decrease in RANTES, IFNα2 and IL-4 cytokine levels in ASD. Overall, ASD presented a distinctive STG cytokine profile with increased pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in the absence of an immune regulatory balance. These data highlights that unique neuroimmune pathways occur in neurodevelopmental disorders such as ASD offering insights into potential therapeutic targets.

secondary.title: Oscillatory Traveling Waves During Visual Entrainment in Autistic and Non-Autistic Adults.
secondary.abstract: Neural oscillations and traveling waves play a crucial role in cognition. In scalp electroencephalography (EEG), waves typically travel along the anterior-posterior axis: forward waves (occipital-to-frontal) predominate during sensory stimulation, while backward waves (frontal-to-occipital) emerge during rest and top-down modulation. Within the predictive coding framework, backward waves reflect predictive signals, whereas forward waves convey sensory processes and prediction errors. In this study, we investigated traveling wave dynamics during a visual entrainment task in non-autistic and autistic adults. Our results show an increase in backward waves during rhythmic visual stimulation in the non-autistic group, consistent with enhanced top-down predictions. Notably, we observed the opposite pattern in the autism group, characterized by a pronounced increase in forward waves at the entrained frequency (ω2 = 0.132). These results align with predictive coding accounts of autistic perception, which hypothesize a difference in balance between predictions and sensory evidence. Specifically, an increase in forward waves may reflect a bias toward sensory signaling over predictive feedback, due to atypical hierarchical communication across brain regions. Together, our findings shed new light on the oscillatory dynamics involved in visual entrainment in non-autistic adults and provide novel evidence in favor of predictive coding accounts of autistic perception.Lay AbstractThe brain continuously processes information by combining incoming sensory signals with prior expectations about the environment. According to predictive coding theories, perception depends on a balance between these two processes: the brain generates predictions about what is likely to happen and then updates those predictions when incoming sensory information does not match expectations. In autism, several theories suggest that this balance may be atypical, with perception relying more strongly on sensory input and less on prior predictions. One way to study how the brain communicates during perception is through 'traveling waves', patterns of rhythmic brain activity that move across the cortex over time. These waves can be measured noninvasively using electroencephalography (EEG). In visual tasks, waves traveling from the back of the brain toward the front are generally linked to the processing of sensory information, whereas waves traveling from the front toward the back are thought to reflect top-down signals such as predictions, expectations, and attentional control. In this study, we investigated traveling brain waves in autistic and non-autistic adults during a visual entrainment task, in which participants viewed rhythmic visual stimulation. We found that non-autistic participants showed an increase in backward traveling waves during stimulation, consistent with stronger predictive or top-down processing. In contrast, autistic participants showed the opposite pattern, with a marked increase in forward traveling waves at the frequency of the visual stimulation. This suggests a greater weighting of incoming sensory signals relative to predictive feedback in autism.

best.title: KCNH1 variants associated with neurodevelopmental disorders exhibit prominent gain of function.
best.abstract: Pathogenic variants in KCNH1, encoding the human ether-á-go-go voltage-gated potassium channel (EAG1, KV10.1), are associated with the neurodevelopmental disorders Temple-Baraitser syndrome (TBS), Zimmermann-Laband syndrome (ZLS), epileptic encephalopathy, and other undefined neurodevelopmental disorders. Investigating the functional consequences of KCNH1 variants can provide information about molecular and cellular pathophysiological mechanisms and help guide therapeutic directions. In this study, we determined the functional properties of 26 disease-associated KCNH1 variants including three recurrent and six that were previously unpublished. Findings were compared to the wildtype (WT) channel along with six rare population variants. Our approach used automated patch clamp recording of heterologously expressed KCNH1 variants in both the homozygous state (variant alone) and the clinically-relevant heterozygous state (variant co-expressed with WT channels). We also examined the impact of alternative splice isoforms on functional consequences of specific variants. We demonstrated that the majority of disease-associated KCNH1 variants exhibit features consistent with gain-of-function including hyperpolarized voltage-dependence of activation, accelerated activation kinetics, or both that promote hyperpolarization of the resting membrane potential. By contrast, one unique variant discovered previously in an autism cohort had a depolarized voltage-dependence of activation and was associated with a depolarized resting potential in cells. Pharmacological testing of KCNH1 variants demonstrated differences in potency for channel block by imipramine and an investigational non-selective potassium channel blocker (LY97241) for specific variants. Collectively, our findings support gain-of-function as the most common, albeit not exclusive, molecular mechanism underlying KCNH1-related disorders and suggest opportunities for potential therapeutic drug repurposing strategies for these conditions.

best.title: Altered stability of dynamic functional architecture in the co-occurrence of autism spectrum disorder and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder.
best.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) frequently co-occur, whereas the underlying neurobiological mechanisms remain largely unexplored. This study aimed to identify alterations in dynamic functional architecture across ASD, ADHD, and their comorbidity. This study selected 287 participants from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange and ADHD-200 datasets, divided into ASD without ADHD (ASD-only), ADHD without ASD (ADHD-only), ASD + ADHD, and typically developing (TD) groups. In this study, we employed dynamic functional stability at the voxel level by measuring the temporal concordance of dynamic functional connectivity (DFC). Furthermore, whole-brain DFC analyses were conducted using clusters with significant stability alterations as seed regions. Group comparisons and correlation analyses were subsequently performed. Our results showed significant group differences in functional stability in the left superior frontal gyrus, orbital part (ORBsup), right pallidum, and left amygdala. Seed-based analyses identified altered DFC variability between the left amygdala and three regions, including the right middle temporal gyrus (MTG), the left insula, and the left superior occipital gyrus (SOG). Notably, DFC variability between the left amygdala and right MTG was significantly negatively correlated with Social Communication Questionnaire (SCQ) scores in the comorbidity group (r = - 0.620, p < 0.01, FDR corrected). From a dynamic perspective, our findings revealed that ASD, ADHD, and their comorbidity exhibited commonanduniquechanges in brain function, thereby enhancing our understanding of the pathogenesis underlying ASD + ADHD.

best.title: Maternal edible THC consumption alters offspring neurodevelopment and emotional behavior in rhesus macaques.
best.abstract: BACKGROUND: Prenatal cannabis exposure is associated with adverse offspring outcomes including altered neurodevelopment. However, there is insufficient evidence to establish a direct association. We sought to determine the impact of chronic prenatal delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) exposure on offspring neurodevelopment and emotional behavior in a translational rhesus macaque model. METHODS: Animals were divided into two groups, control and THC-exposed, with both groups receiving a daily edible (placebo or THC) pre-conception, throughout pregnancy, and postnatally. MRI was performed longitudinally across gestation and infancy to assess volumetric and microstructural brain development. Serial behavioral testing, including motor and emotional assessments, was performed postnatally. At 6 months of age, brain tissue was collected for histology, immunohistochemistry (IHC), whole genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS), and bulk RNA-sequencing. FINDINGS: Analysis of the MRI images showed white matter changes with higher fractional anisotropy in the corpus callosum (CC) and centrum semiovale in THC-exposed infants. However, there were no significant differences in regional brain volumes. Behavioral testing demonstrated that THC-exposed infants displayed increased vocalizations and decreased independence. WGBS identified differentially methylated regions (DMRs) associated with THC exposure in the cerebellum and prefrontal cortex, annotated to genes involved in synaptic organization and brain development. RNA-sequencing confirmed differential expression of genes related to axon development and glutamatergic synapse, with expression correlating with methylation levels. INTERPRETATION: Chronic prenatal edible THC exposure in the rhesus macaque was associated with changes in white matter development, effects on infant behavior with signs of increased stress and anxiety, and brain DNA methylation and expression of genes involved in neurodevelopment. best.title: Domain-associated phenotypic patterns with MACF1 variants.
best.abstract: PURPOSE: While heterozygous de novo missense variants in the microtubule-binding GAR domain of Microtubule-actin cross-linking factor 1 (MACF1) cause Lissencephaly 9 with Complex Brainstem Malformations (LIS9) [MIM 618325], the phenotypic impact of variants outside this domain remains unclear. METHODS: We assembled a cohort of 5 affected individuals from 4 unrelated families with biallelic non-GAR domain MACF1 variants who exhibit partially overlapping yet unique phenotypic traits. A sixth individual with a de novo, heterozygous frameshift variant was additionally identified. Combined with previously reported cases, we analyzed genotype and phenotype data from 22 individuals using Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO)-based unsupervised hierarchical clustering. RESULTS: Clustering revealed two distinct phenotypic signatures, suggesting domain-associated effects. Variants outside the GAR domain associate with broader neurodevelopmental phenotypes and craniofacial and skeletal involvement. Enrichment analysis (p < 0.001) using OMIM HPO sets supported these findings. In contrast to the GAR domain's strong correlation with LIS9, biallelic non-GAR domain MACF1 variants were linked to distinct developmental anomalies. CONCLUSION: These results expand the phenotypic spectrum of MACF1-related disorders and provide preliminary evidence for domain-associated MACF1 variant effects. While limited by sample size and lack of functional validation, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and underscore the utility of HPO-based clustering for systematic phenotype comparison as additional cases emerge. Comprehensive genetic and phenotypic assessments are essential for understanding the role of MACF1 in development, informing diagnosis, and guiding future research on cytoskeletal regulation in neurodevelopment.

best.title: Altered medial prefrontal-striatal connectivity and plasticity in humanized CBLN2 mice.
best.abstract: Deciphering processes that are responsible for differences in brain development and architecture among species may provide clues to the species-specific program and may facilitate a mechanistic understanding of vulnerability to neuropsychiatric disorders. It has recently been shown that the promoter of the CBLN2 gene, which codes for a synaptogenic factor, cerebellin 2 (Cbln2), has a repressor element in mice but not in humans. A humanized mouse lacking this repressor (hCbln2) reproduces higher spine density in medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) neurons and higher corticothalamic connectivity observed in humans. Cbln2 is part of a trans-synaptic complex that includes glutamate delta-1 receptor (GluD1) and neurexins (Nrxn) (GluD1-Cbln2-Nrxn). Interestingly, we have previously reported a contrasting striatal patch-matrix expression pattern of GluD1 in mouse versus monkey, suggesting a potential role of the GluD1-Cbln complex in species differences. In this study, we examined the synaptic organization and function in the cortex and dorsal striatum of hCbln2 mice. Consistent with previous reports, hCbln2 mice exhibited increased vGluT1 expression in the mPFC, indicating enhanced intracortical connectivity. Electrophysiological recordings further revealed an increased mEPSC frequency along with a reduced mIPSC frequency in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons, suggesting an increase in excitatory/inhibitory balance. These changes were accompanied by enhanced mTOR signalling and autophagic deficits in the mPFC. Contrasting synaptic changes were observed in the striatum with an increase in vGluT2 and a reduction in vGluT1, together with a decrease in GluD1-Cbln1 and an increase in hevin. Importantly, corticostriatal dysfunction characterized by a reduction in cortical contribution to mEPSCs and impaired DHPG-induced synaptic depression was observed in the hCbln2 medium spiny neurons. Further, hCbln2 mice displayed increased repetitive behaviour together with social and affective-like deficits, consistent with autism-relevant phenotypes. Collectively, these findings identify humanized Cbln2 regulation as a driver of divergent cortical and striatal synaptic remodelling, disrupted corticostriatal synaptic function, and behavioural abnormalities relevant to neurodevelopmental disorders.

best.title: Neonatal-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy: High genetic yield and long-term outcomes in a multicenter southern European cohort.
best.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To determine the genetic diagnostic yield, characterize the clinical and genetic landscape, and evaluate long-term epilepsy, neurodevelopmental, and survival outcomes in a strictly defined cohort of neonatal-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE). METHODS: Retrospective multicenter observational study across tertiary epilepsy centers in Italy, Greece, and Spain. Sixty-two full-term neonates fulfilling ILAE 2022 criteria for DEE with seizure onset within the first 30 days of life and a minimum follow-up of 18 months were included. All patients underwent next-generation sequencing-based genetic testing. Genetic findings, clinical characteristics, and long-term outcomes were systematically analyzed. RESULTS: A molecular diagnosis was established in 82.2% of patients (51/62), identifying variants across 29 genes grouped, for descriptive purposes, into four broad categories according to principal biological role. First-line whole-exome sequencing achieved higher diagnostic yield than targeted gene panels (88.9% vs. 41.2%), although this comparison was influenced by differences in testing era and strategy. KCNQ2 variants were the most frequent genetic cause (29.4%), and several treatable metabolic disorders were identified. After a mean follow-up of 11.9 years, 64.5% of patients had drug-resistant epilepsy and mortality reached 17.7%. Seizure freedom was achieved in a subset of patients, particularly those with KCNQ2-related DEE. Nevertheless, severe-to-profound intellectual disability affected 71.7% of evaluable patients and persisted even among those who became seizure-free, suggesting that neurodevelopmental outcomes are influenced by factors beyond seizure burden, including the underlying genetic disorder and other disease-related factors. However, the marked variability observed precludes any causal inference from these data. SIGNIFICANCE: This large European cohort demonstrates a high genetic diagnostic yield in neonatal-onset DEE, supporting first-line whole-exome sequencing as the preferred first-tier genetic test. The persistence of severe neurodevelopmental impairment despite seizure control highlights the need for precision therapies targeting disease mechanisms in addition to seizure management. PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: We studied 62 newborns who developed severe epilepsy caused by genetic changes, following them for up to 25 years. We found a genetic cause in over 80% of cases, and genetic testing that reads the entire genetic code was far more effective than tests that only look at specific genes. Although seizures improved in some children over time, nearly all had lasting intellectual disability regardless of seizure control. This suggests that the underlying genetic condition may contribute substantially to brain development in addition to the effects of seizures, although our study cannot determine the relative contribution of each factor.
