secondary.title: Novel cell markers with altered expression in brain aging and Alzheimer's disease: A review.
secondary.abstract: Aging and Alzheimer's disease are complex processes marked by continuous neuronal loss, disrupted neural networks, and cognitive decline. The past decade has seen advances in genomics, proteomics, and single-cell RNA sequencing, enabling the discovery of cellular markers with distinct gene expression patterns. This review aims to compile recent markers of aging and Alzheimer's disease in immune, glial, and neuronal cells, which are increasingly vital for enhancing diagnostic precision and monitoring disease progression. Markers such as Triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2) and Cluster of differentiation 33 (CD33) facilitate immune responses and function as indicators of neuroinflammation and amyloid-beta clearance; Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and aquaporin-4 serve as indicators of gliosis and impaired interstitial fluid drainage; Postsynaptic density protein 95 (PSD-95), Synaptosomal-associated protein 25 (SNAP25), and aberrant tau phosphorylation signify synaptic degradation and cytoskeletal instability characteristic of Alzheimer's pathology. The breakdown of the blood-brain barrier is associated with endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) and vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM-1). The markers were identified using cutting-edge technologies that unveiled variations in gene expression across cell types, brain regions, and disease stages. This cellular heterogeneity improves understanding of Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression and brain aging, clarifies molecular pathways, and may be used for prognostic and diagnostic purposes after thorough validation. Novel cellular markers with altered expression profiles are still being identified through ongoing research, which could be crucial for improving our understanding of and ability to treat neurodegenerative diseases.

secondary.title: The spectrum within the spectrum: Neural heterogeneity in autism.
secondary.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) encompasses diverse behavioral, cognitive, and neural profiles that vary widely across individuals. Because diagnosis remains predominantly behavior-based, clinically meaningful within-spectrum differences are often missed. Recent advances in neuroimaging analysis have created opportunities for the identification of distinct neural profiles within ASD. These new avenues provide ways to examine intra-ASD heterogeneity directly, identifying person-specific brain-behavior patterns that group-level comparisons fail to capture. The present systematic review focused on neuroimaging methods (i.e., resting-state fMRI; rs-fMRI, cortical morphology) that emphasized heterogeneity-informed outcomes based on normative modeling, data-driven subtyping, clustering analysis and similar analytic choices. For rs-fMRI, findings showed that differences in connectivity within the default mode and salience networks were linked to social-communication and language impairments, with subtype-specific patterns emerging across samples. In cortical thickness and surface area, studies identified distinct developmental trajectories and individual deviation profiles, with prefrontal and temporal regions often tied to repetitive behaviors and social-communication difficulties. Voxel-based analyses revealed subgroup-specific gray matter alterations, including cerebellar and cortical differences, that aligned with variation in repetitive behaviors and social difficulties. Collectively, this emerging evidence supports the notion that neural heterogeneity in autism is a core feature rather than a limitation. Embracing individual variability can provide crucial insight into the inconsistencies and contradictions of earlier case-control and group-level findings. Moving forward, autism research must prioritize heterogeneity-based methods to establish reproducible subtypes and individualized brain-behavior links.

secondary.title: TLDc proteins: Stress-responsive nexus regulators of redox signaling, V-ATPase dynamics, and organellar crosstalk in neurodegeneration.
secondary.abstract: Many age-related neurodegenerative disorders are marked by progressive defects in cellular energy metabolism and protein homeostasis that converge on mitochondrial and lysosomal dysfunction. TLDc domain-containing proteins, such as OXR1, NCOA7, and related family members, have emerged as crucial modulators of organellar physiology and cellular stress responses. Growing evidence indicates that TLDc proteins physically interact with vacuolar ATPases (V-ATPases) to modulate their assembly and catalytic activity, linking TLDc function directly to the maintenance of lysosomal and Golgi lumen pH. This organellar pH homeostasis, in turn, is fundamental to intracellular iron handling and metabolic regulation, processes essential for mitochondrial bioenergetics, lysosomal functions, and cellular viability. Lysosomes maintain an acidic lumen via V-ATPase proton pumping, counterbalanced by specific ion channels, including TMEM175. This acidic environment is required for ferric iron reduction and subsequent release into the cytosol; when acidification fails, cells develop cytosolic iron deficiency, mitochondrial defects, pseudohypoxia via HIF-1α activation, and inflammation. Conversely, iron flux from lysosomes to mitochondria depends on acidic conditions and direct organelle contact, as exemplified by BDH2-driven siderophore transport, a V-ATPase-dependent but not TLDc-regulated process, which supports mitochondrial bioenergetics and sustains lysosomal acidity. Iron and pH dysregulation synergize to drive ferroptosis, lipid peroxidation, and neurotoxicity. Emerging studies link lysosomal deacidification and iron dyshomeostasis to the pathogenesis of major neurodegenerative diseases. These mechanisms collectively shape neuronal resilience, survival, and aging trajectories. This review integrates recent insights into how TLDc proteins coordinate organellar pH regulation and iron homeostasis and discusses how disruption of these interconnected pathways contributes to age-related neurodegeneration.

secondary.title: Nanoplastics as disruptors of microtubule dynamics and intracellular trafficking: implications for cellular senescence and ageing.
secondary.abstract: Nanoplastics (NPs) are increasingly recognized as persistent intracellular cargoes whose long-term effects may depend not only on chemical reactivity, oxidative stress, and inflammation, but also on how particle-containing vesicles are transported, positioned, and cleared. Because the positioning and movement of endosomes, lysosomes, autophagosomes, mitochondria, and NP-containing vesicles are extensively regulated by microtubule-based transport, prolonged NP retention has the potential to disrupt intracellular trafficking and organelle homeostasis. Here, we examine how NPs may influence microtubule dynamics, tubulin post-translational modifications, motor-dependent trafficking, and organelle positioning, with particular emphasis on their relationships to cellular senescence and ageing. We first summarize evidence that senescence and ageing are associated with alterations in microtubule organization, stability, acetylation, intracellular transport capacity, cytoplasmic physical properties, and neuronal microtubule integrity. We then evaluate emerging evidence linking NP exposure to altered microtubule states and trafficking-related dysfunction, while considering particle size, shape, surface chemistry, aggregation, exposure duration, and intracellular burden as important determinants of particle fate and cellular response. We propose microtubule-dependent trafficking congestion as a testable framework in which persistent NP-containing cargo progressively reduces intracellular transport efficiency, while distinguishing this state from simple particle retention or generalized organelle dysfunction. Potential mechanisms include increased cargo loading, altered kinesin-dynein balance, perinuclear lysosomal retention, changes in cytoplasmic crowding or viscosity, and dysregulation of tubulin-modifying enzymes. Direct evidence for NP-induced trafficking congestion remains limited, highlighting the need for quantitative live-cell measurements of vesicle mobility, velocity, run length, pausing, directionality, and recovery after exposure withdrawal. Finally, we discuss human biomonitoring and tissue-distribution evidence and emphasize the distinction between detection of plastic particles in human tissues and demonstration of pathological causality.

secondary.title: Exploring shared genetic pathways and gene interplay in major neurodegenerative diseases: a comprehensive review.
secondary.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are progressive disorders that involve the loss and dysfunction of neurons. Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Huntington's disease, Frontotemporal dementia are examples of diseases. While different clinically, these disorders have a common genetic, molecular and cellular basis. This review examines the common genetic pathways, along with the interactions between genes of major neurodegenerative diseases, with a focus on the key genes, such as APOE, SNCA, MAPT, TARDBP, LRRK2 and HTT. The common pathogenic mechanisms considered to play a major role in disease progression include protein misfolding and aggregation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, diminished autophagy, and impaired lysosomal function, as well as synaptic degeneration. The review also emphasizes the role of systems biology strategies, such as genome-wide association studies, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, interactome analysis, and multi-omics integration, to unveiling complex molecular networks in neurodegeneration. Furthermore, the emerging biomarker strategies and therapeutic strategies targeting convergence signaling pathways including NF-κB, PI3K-Akt-mTOR, MAPK and Wnt/β-catenin are summarized. The common genetic basis and the cross-connecting molecular mechanisms of the various neurodegenerative diseases could help in the discovery of new biomarkers and pan-therapeutic targets. Further advances in molecular genetics, computational biology and precision medicine are needed to enhance early detection and the creation of effective disease-modifying treatments.

secondary.title: Neuroprotective roles of Klotho signaling in Huntington's disease: From molecular insights to clinical translation.
secondary.abstract: Huntington's Disease (HD) is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene, producing toxic mutant huntingtin (mHTT) protein. This leads to progressive motor dysfunction, cognitive decline, and psychiatric disturbances. Despite advances in understanding mHTT toxicity, potentially disease-modifying therapies remain scarce, underscoring the need for novel approaches targeting core pathophysiological mechanisms. Klotho, a multifunctional anti-aging protein, regulates several pathways relevant to neuronal survival and may have relevance to HD pathophysiology. Klotho is a co-receptor with a membrane and is a soluble co-receptor that regulates synaptic and metabolic homeostasis. Although direct experimental evidence in HD remains limited, emerging findings from aging and neurodegeneration research suggest that Klotho-mediated pathways may influence mechanisms relevant to HD pathogenesis. It suppresses fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) signaling and major pathways such as PI3K/Akt-FOXO, Wnt/ -catenin and insulin/IGF-1 pathways, which oppose the hallmarks of HD, namely excitotoxicity, calcium dysregulation, impaired neuroprotection, and peripheral neuroinflammation. There is growing evidence of the involvement of Klotho in mitochondrial health and biogenesis, mitophagy coordination, and oxidative stress resistance - direct mitigating cellular toxicity caused by mHTT. These mechanistic overlaps suggest that Klotho signaling may represent a potential area for investigation in HD. It deals with oxidative stress, excitotoxicity, inflammation, and metabolic dysregulation, and compares it to other diseases of the neurodegenerative type in which Klotho deficits contribute to pathology. Such a structure encourages Klotho-based interventions as a new, mechanism-based approach to HD. Further experimental studies are required to determine whether modulation of Klotho signaling could influence disease progression in HD.

secondary.title: Axonemal dynein gene dysfunction as a cause of male infertility: insights from DNAH family mutations.
secondary.abstract: Male infertility is a complex disorder and defective sperm motility is one of the most common reasons for impaired fertility. The dynein axonemal heavy chain (DNAH) gene family encode molecular motors that form the structure of cilia and sperm flagella. Abnormalities in several DNAH genes have already been confirmed to be causative factors responsible for male infertility conditions, mainly including asthenozoospermia, multiple morphological abnormalities of the sperm flagella (MMAF), and reproductive failure related to primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD). Here, this review illustrates the current evidence regarding the involvement of members of the DNAH family in male infertility, along with summarizing their biological functions, genotypic and phenotypic correlations and clinical significance. Due to the breakthroughs of the technologies of whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing along with research with animal models and functional investigations, the diversity of reported causative DNAH mutations and their implications for the organization and function of sperm axonemes are currently better understood. DNAH1, DNAH8 and DNAH17 are the DNAH genes most frequently described as being involved in male infertility, though growing evidence also indicated that DNAH3, DNAH11, DNAH12 and DNAH14 also contribute to the male reproductive disorders. Implementation of testing DNAH genes into molecular diagnostics enhances the assessment of genes causing severe sperm motility disorders and aids genetic counseling of the affected families. Together with the genomic and functional data, further research will elucidate additional details for disease mechanisms and will bring benefit to more precise diagnosis and treatments of DNAH-associated male infertility.

secondary.title: Dysfunction of lipid metabolism and lysosomal capacity: at the core of microglial aging?
secondary.abstract: As primary immune cells of the central nervous system (CNS), microglia maintain immune surveillance, inflammation regulation, cell interactions and debris clearance. These dynamic and adaptive effector functions are reciprocally sustained by microglial metabolism. Lipids are emerging as a key programmer of microglial metabolic and functional flexibility in conditions of homeostasis, cellular stress, and pathology. The delicate equilibrium in microglial lipid homeostasis is dependent on the integrated activity of all cellular components, including the lysosome-lipophagy pathway. Continuous adaptations in microglial metabolism contribute to a cumulative imbalance between lysosomal network capacity and the efficacy of lipid turnover in aged microglia. The disequilibrium contributes to microglial fatigue and detrimental homeostatic activity associated with aging. Lipid droplet-accumulating microglia (LDAM) emerged as an age-associated example of these lysosome-lipid flux alterations. While characterized by dysregulated phagocytosis and pro-inflammatory intercellular signaling, the role of LDAM in the contexts of neuroplasticity, aging-related cognitive decline and frailty remains undetermined. This review discusses the immunometabolic profile of aging LDAM and their interactions with neurons and synapses, highlighting the impact of intercellular lipid signaling route.

secondary.title: Human Brain Organoid-Enabling Discoveries Reach the Clinic: A Translational Inflection Point.
secondary.abstract: Human brain organoids have evolved from early neurodevelopmental models into platforms for therapeutic discovery. Here, we highlight two cases in which organoid-derived findings enabled FDA-approved clinical trials. Patient-derived organoids modeling Pitt-Hopkins syndrome revealed human-specific, TCF4-dependent abnormalities and supported the development of a regulated AAV gene therapy. In parallel, Rett syndrome organoids cultured aboard the International Space Station uncovered space-induced neural senescence, characterized by retroelement-associated neuroinflammation, prompting evaluation of antiretroviral therapy. These examples illustrate how organoids can reveal disease mechanisms that are inaccessible or incompletely reproduced in animal models, while animal studies remain essential for validation and safety assessment. As the field advances, matching model complexity to experimental purpose-and ensuring reproducibility, scalability, and accessibility-will be critical. Human brain organoids are crossing a translational threshold, emerging as engines of therapeutic discovery and gateways to clinical intervention.

secondary.title: Pathogenesis and therapeutic targets of neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease mediated by microglia lysosomal dysfunction.
secondary.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder characterized by two core pathological features: senile plaques formed by amyloid-β protein (Aβ) deposits and neurofibrillary tangles formed by hyperphosphorylated tau protein. In recent years, neuroinflammation has been recognized as a key driver in the pathogenesis of AD, and microglia, as innate immune cells of the central nervous system, play a central role in regulating the onset and progression of neuroinflammation. Lysosomes are key organelles within microglia responsible for degrading pathological proteins and regulating inflammatory signaling; dysfunction of lysosomes in microglia severely impairs their ability to clear Aβ, damaged proteins, and cellular debris, thereby promoting inflammatory responses. This manuscript summarizes upstream mechanisms that may influence microglial lysosomal dysfunction from four perspectives: pathological proteins, genetic factors, lipid metabolism disorders, and proinflammatory cytokines. Pathological proteins can impair lysosomal acidification and biogenesis by interfering with key pathways such as the TFEB-v-ATPase axis; various genetic factors exacerbate functional dysregulation by influencing the expression of lysosome-related genes and lipid metabolism; lipid metabolism disorders promote lysosomal membrane permeabilization, block the autophagy cascade and activate the inflammasome; proinflammatory cytokines can exert varying effects on the clearance of pathological substrates and by regulating lysosomal function. The aforementioned factors can influence microglial lysosomal function through various mechanisms, thereby contributing to impaired clearance of pathological substrates and the onset and progression of neuroinflammation. Intervention strategies targeting microglial lysosomal dysfunction, including enhancing lysosomal degradation capacity, regulating autophagy related pathways, correcting cellular metabolic dysregulation and suppressing excessive neuroinflammation, may offer new avenues for AD treatment.

secondary.title: Dysfunction of the blood-brain barrier and neurovascular unit in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis - From advanced human models to treatments.
secondary.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder, characterized by the degeneration of motor neurons, resulting in progressive and eventually complete loss of motor function. The phenotypical heterogeneity of ALS poses a challenge to early diagnosis and treatment, with currently available therapeutics only capable of relieving symptoms and slowing progression. While ALS is classified as a motor neuron disease (MND), research has identified significant impairment to the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and neurovascular unit (NVU) of ALS patients. The BBB along with supporting cells of the NVU selectively control the entry of substances into the central nervous system (CNS) and maintain brain homeostasis, with its many cellular components demonstrating impaired function, specifically relating to inflammation, oxidative stress and TDP-43 proteinopathy. The advent of more advanced in vitro techniques as well as use of patient-derived BBB cells has presented a promising alternative to recreate the in vivo structure of the BBB/NVU in a highly controlled platform. Such approaches have ranged from simple 2-dimensional (2D) cell culture to intricate 3-dimensional (3D) co-culture systems, as well as microfluidic systems and organoids, with a potential to investigate ALS associated BBB/NVU dysfunction and drug discovery. This review provides a comprehensive assessment of known BBB/NVU dysfunction in ALS and methods of investigating this using in vitro and in vivo platforms with a focus on inflammation, oxidative stress and pathological TDP-43 expression. This review also presents a future perspective to overcoming barriers to treatment of ALS using new patient-derived BBB/NVU model systems.

secondary.title: Cytochrome P450-mediated vitamin D and cholesterol metabolism in the pathophysiology of neurodevelopmental disorders.
secondary.abstract: Cytochrome P450 (CYP450) enzymes play critical roles in the pathophysiology of neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), including autism spectrum disorder (ASD), Rett syndrome (RTT), and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Although traditionally associated with hepatic and intestinal xenobiotic metabolism, several CYP450 isoforms are expressed in the central nervous system, where they regulate essential pathways involving vitamin D and cholesterol-two molecules fundamental to neural development, synaptogenesis, and membrane homeostasis. The cholesterol-CYP27A1-27-hydroxycholesterol (27-OHC)-liver X receptor (LXR) axis has emerged as a critical regulator of neurodevelopment, influencing INSIG proteins, LXRs, and LDL receptors. Additionally, members of the CYP1A, CYP2B, CYP2C, and CYP3A families contribute to neuroendocrine balance and fetal brain maturation. Dysregulation of these pathways may contribute to synaptic dysfunction, neuronal hyperexcitability, and metabolic imbalance observed in NDDs. This review highlights the interplay between CYP450 enzymes, vitamin D metabolism, and cholesterol homeostasis, emphasizing their mechanistic relevance in ASD and related disorders, and discusses the therapeutic potential of targeting CYP450-mediated pathways to restore metabolic and neurodevelopmental equilibrium.

secondary.title: The early MALDI years and how "microscopy-grade" transmission-mode MALDI-2 mass spectrometry imaging was realized after a long delay: a personal retrospective and review.
secondary.abstract: Since its invention in the mid-1980s, matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization (MALDI) mass spectrometry (MS) has developed into a key bioanalytical technique for numerous research areas in the life sciences. One remarkable application shift that began in the mid-1990s is the increasing use of the label-free MALDI technique as a molecular microscope. One holy grail of MALDI-MS Imaging (MALDI-MSI) is to reach a true single-cell or even a sub-cellular resolution to visualize the molecular content of individual cells and organelles thereof. This requires pixel sizes in the low to sub-micrometer range. These are difficult to achieve, such that new irradiation concepts are needed. Another contemporary research focus is on the advancement of multimodal imaging, especially in the combination of immunofluorescence (IF) microscopy and highly-resolved MALDI-MSI. Drawing upon four decades of active research in the MALDI field, I structured this review to offer both a personal (retro-)perspective and a comprehensive exploration of both historical and contemporary aspects. The initial chapter provides a historical overview of the development of the first laser microprobe mass analyzer (LAMMA 500), while the subsequent chapter chronicles the discovery of the MALDI technique and its initial applications in biological research. The third and fourth sections then direct the reader's attention to selected recent advancements in MALDI-imaging, highlighting pioneering contributions from both in-house and external laboratories. These developments include the utilization of laser postionization for MALDI-2 and the resurgence of the LAMMA 500 concept in the form of transmission (t-) mode MALDI-2. The recently introduced direct coupling of t-MALDI-2 with IF microscopy holds significant promise in unveiling novel avenues for cell biology research.

secondary.title: NF-κB across the Alzheimer disease spectrum: Context-dependent protective and pathogenic roles.
secondary.abstract: Nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) has been implicated in both protective and detrimental processes in Alzheimer disease (AD), creating an apparent contradiction in the literature. Increasing evidence, however, indicates that these divergent effects reflect differences in cell type, molecular configuration, activation kinetics, disease state, and the surrounding pathological environment rather than a true biological paradox. Under transient and tightly regulated conditions, NF-κB can support neuronal survival, stress adaptation, antioxidant defense, and selected compensatory responses to amyloid-β pathology. In contrast, persistent or disease-conditioned signaling is more consistently associated with amyloidogenic processing, tau propagation, chronic neuroinflammation, impaired proteostasis, neuronal dysfunction, and neurovascular injury. The available evidence therefore supports an asymmetric framework in which protective effects are confined to relatively specific molecular and temporal settings, whereas sustained pathological signaling is supported across a broader range of disease-relevant models and cellular processes. This distinction argues against indiscriminate activation or global inhibition of NF-κB, either of which could disrupt physiological functions while failing to selectively suppress disease-driving pathways. Therapeutic strategies should instead target defined pathological NF-κB programs within the relevant cell type and disease context while preserving adaptive and homeostatic signaling. This review synthesizes the context-dependent roles of NF-κB in AD and provides a framework for reconciling its apparently opposing effects.

secondary.title: Nitric oxide signaling and mitophagy in Parkinson's disease: implications for aerobic exercise-related neuroprotection.
secondary.abstract: Parkinson's disease is strongly associated with mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired mitochondrial quality control, including defective mitophagy. Aerobic exercise is increasingly recognized as a safe and accessible intervention that can improve motor and non-motor outcomes in Parkinson's disease and may also engage mechanisms relevant to disease modification. In this review, we propose a context-dependent framework in which aerobic exercise reshapes nitric oxide signaling toward a more adaptive profile, characterized by relatively moderate, transient, and spatially restricted nitric oxide bioactivity, and we discuss how this shift may influence mitochondrial biogenesis, mitophagy initiation, and autophagic flux regulation. Rather than treating nitric oxide as uniformly protective or deleterious, we argue that its biological effects in Parkinson's disease depend on source, concentration, duration, subcellular localization, cellular target, and surrounding redox milieu. However, direct evidence that exercise-derived nitric oxide activates these pathways in Parkinson's disease-relevant neural tissue is still limited. We further highlight major translational gaps, including cell-type and brain-region heterogeneity, incomplete definition of exercise dose-response relationships, and the lack of validated in vivo biomarkers of neuronal mitophagy and nitric oxide dynamics in patients with Parkinson's disease. Overall, aerobic exercise is a plausible modulator of mitophagy-related pathways in Parkinson's disease, and nitric oxide is a credible contributor to this effect; however, the current evidence supports a multi-node, context-dependent model rather than a simple linear mechanism.

secondary.title: VPS13C-mediated endoplasmic reticulum-lysosome tethering in neuronal stress responses.
secondary.abstract: Organelle contact sites are increasingly recognized as regulatory interfaces that coordinate lipid transfer, ion signaling, and metabolic adaptation. In neurons, communication among the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), lysosomes, and mitochondria is essential for cellular homeostasis. Recent studies have identified vacuolar protein sorting 13 homolog C (VPS13C), a lipid transport protein, as a key mediator of ER-lysosome tethering and as an important component of the response to lysosomal stress. Structural analyses show that VPS13 family proteins form elongated lipid transport channels that are proposed to facilitate phospholipid transfer between adjacent membranes. Following lysosomal damage, VPS13C is recruited to ER-lysosome contact interfaces, where it forms tethering bridges that may support membrane repair by enabling high-capacity lipid transfer from the ER to lysosomal membranes. Beyond membrane repair, these contact interfaces may also participate in broader organelle communication networks. ER-lysosome contacts can occur in proximity to ER-mitochondria junctions, potentially forming multi organelle signaling hubs that coordinate lipid redistribution, calcium signaling, and mitochondrial adaptation. These signals may influence downstream responses, including activation of TFEB and TFE3, which regulate lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. Disruption of this contact site network has emerged as a potential contributor to Parkinson's disease. Loss of VPS13C function is associated with altered lysosomal homeostasis and intersects with pathogenic pathways involving α-synuclein aggregation, PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy, and LRRK2 signaling. This review presents a framework in which ER-lysosome tethering is considered part of a staged cellular damage response linking membrane repair, metabolic coordination, and transcriptional adaptation.

secondary.title: Traumatic brain injury: Multi-omics insights into brain aging, neurodegeneration, and precision therapeutics.
secondary.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of mortality and persistent neurological disability and is increasingly recognized as a potential contributor to accelerated brain aging and long-term neurodegenerative processes. Beyond the immediate mechanical insult, TBI initiates dynamic secondary injury cascades involving chronic neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, synaptic and axonal degeneration, metabolic disturbances, and blood-brain barrier disruption. The persistence and temporal evolution of these molecular alterations may interact with intrinsic aging mechanisms, contributing to progressive neuronal dysfunction and increased vulnerability to age-associated neurodegenerative disorders. The marked biological and temporal heterogeneity of TBI therefore presents major challenges for conventional diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic approaches. Recent advances in multi-omics technologies, including genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, lipidomics, and single-cell and spatial approaches, offer unprecedented opportunities to characterize the molecular trajectories linking TBI, brain aging, and neurodegeneration. Integrative multi-omics frameworks, coupled with network biology, artificial intelligence, machine learning, and causal inference, enable the identification of molecular signatures, age-related regulatory networks, clinically relevant biomarkers, and therapeutically actionable targets. This review synthesizes emerging multi-omics insights into the molecular mechanisms through which TBI may influence brain aging and neurodegenerative progression, with particular emphasis on phase-specific molecular signatures, biomarker discovery, patient stratification, therapeutic target prioritization, and precision neurotherapeutics. We further discuss longitudinal profiling, single-cell and spatial approaches, and AI-assisted modeling for patient stratification and therapeutic optimization. Integrating multi-omics with systems biology may provide a framework for studying TBI-associated brain aging and developing personalized interventions, although prospective clinical validation remains essential.

secondary.title: Cortical transcriptomic dysregulation in Autism spectrum disorder: A conceptual synthesis.
secondary.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition in which human post-mortem cortical transcriptomic studies have identified recurrent but context-sensitive molecular abnormalities. This narrative review synthesises RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) evidence from ASD cortex and organises recurrent findings into three interacting cortical domains: synaptic/neuronal programmes, immune-glial programmes, and RNA-regulatory processes. Across bulk cortical datasets, the most reproducible signals include relative downregulation of neuronal and synaptic expression programmes together with upregulation of glial-associated and neuroimmune signatures, whereas transcript-level analyses further implicate alternative splicing, microexon dysregulation, differential transcript usage, and isoform-level perturbation. Single-nucleus and related cell-resolved approaches localise these abnormalities to defined neuronal and glial populations, while long-read strategies strengthen inference on transcript structure and isoform complexity. Within this framework, mitochondrial-related findings are best interpreted as a linked bioenergetic component rather than an equally established standalone transcriptomic domain. The review also summarise the principal interpretive constraints of cortical ASD transcriptomics, including region specificity, developmental stage, cohort heterogeneity, cell-type composition, post-mortem tissue quality, and cross-platform comparability.

secondary.title: Disruptions in axonal lysosome transport and its contribution to neurological disease.
secondary.abstract: Lysosomes are central to the maintenance of protein and organelle homeostasis in cells. Optimal lysosome function is particularly critical for neurons which are long-lived, non-dividing and highly polarized with specialized compartments such as axons and dendrites with distinct architecture, cargo, and turnover requirements. In recent years, there has been a growing appreciation for the role played by axonal lysosome transport in regulating neuronal development, its maintenance and functioning. Perturbations to optimal axonal lysosome abundance leading to either strong accumulations or dearth of lysosomes are both linked to altered neuronal health and functioning. In this review we highlight how two critical regulators of axonal lysosome transport and abundance, the small GTPase Arl8 and the adaptor protein JIP3, aid in maintaining axonal lysosome homeostasis and how alterations to their levels and activity could contribute to neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative diseases.

secondary.title: From patient cells to patient therapy: Twenty years of iPSC-based translation in neurodegenerative disease.
secondary.abstract: Twenty years after the discovery of induced pluripotent stem cells, the field has progressed from patient-specific disease modeling toward cell-based therapies for neurodegenerative disorders. Parkinson's disease has emerged as the leading model for neuronal replacement, whereas Huntington's disease, Alzheimer's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis require distinct combinations of circuit reconstruction, cellular support, immune modulation, and engineered therapeutic delivery. We discuss key determinants of clinical translation, including cell source, product identity, graft composition, graft-host interactions, manufacturing reproducibility, genomic integrity, and clinical evaluation. We propose that the interval between cell transplantation and long-term engraftment constitutes a biological "black box" in which graft fate and therapeutic outcome are determined. As regenerative medicine enters its third decade, future progress will depend not only on generating therapeutic cells but also on elucidating and engineering the biological processes that determine their fate after transplantation, marking a conceptual transition from stem cell biology toward transplantation biology.

secondary.title: The redox paradox in neurological disorders: balancing cytoprotection, ferroptosis, and therapeutic targeting.
secondary.abstract: Neurological disorders, including ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke, traumatic brain injury, and chronic neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and multiple sclerosis, represent a major global health burden. Despite diverse etiologies, these conditions share common pathological mechanisms driven by oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, iron dysregulation, and secondary neuronal injury. The nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) signalling cascade and its downstream target heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) are master regulators of cellular redox homeostasis. HO-1 plays a pivotal yet dichotomous role: its products biliverdin/bilirubin and carbon monoxide exert antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-apoptotic effects, whereas excessive HO-1 induction can exacerbate iron-mediated oxidative injury and ferroptosis through the release of redox-active ferrous iron. Rather than cataloguing protective studies, this review builds a contextual framework that specifies when HO-1 activation is protective versus detrimental, organised around three converging determinants: cell-type specificity, iron-handling capacity, and disease stage. We extend this framework to the often-overlooked dimensions of sex, age, and model heterogeneity, and use it to interrogate conflicting findings across the literature. We further dissect how Nrf2/HO-1 regulates ferroptosis through the GPX4-ACSL4-SLC7A11 axis, critically appraise the largely unexamined relationship between Nrf2 and the parallel FSP1/CoQ10, GCH1/BH4, and DHODH defence systems, and distil lessons from clinical trials of Nrf2 activators. The goal is an analytical account that identifies where the evidence is robust, where it is contradictory, and where the principal research gaps lie.

secondary.title: Integrative transcriptomic and machine learning analysis identifies S100A8 as a key hub bridging peripheral inflammation and synaptic deficits in schizophrenia.
secondary.abstract: Schizophrenia (SCZ) involves immune dysregulation and synaptic deficits, yet the molecular link between peripheral inflammation and central synaptic pathology remains unclear. We integrated blood transcriptomes from four SCZ cohorts (478 samples: 245 patients, 233 controls) and validated findings in single-cell brain data and an ELNI mouse model. After batch correction, 272 genes were differentially expressed, with S100A8 as the top upregulated immune gene. WGCNA identified a disease-associated module (blue, 133 genes, r = 0.16, p = 7 × 10⁻⁴) containing S100A8; its intersection with differentially expressed genes yielded 44 key genes enriched for cytoplasmic translation, mitochondrial electron transport, and innate immunity. Machine learning ranked S100A8 as the top discriminative feature, and its upregulation was robust across four independent analytic pipelines. CIBERSORTx revealed increased neutrophils and decreased regulatory T and resting NK cells in patients, with S100A8 correlating positively with neutrophils. Single-cell analysis showed that S100A8-expressing cells were specifically expanded in microglia (2.98% → 3.94%, OR = 1.34), and S100A8⁺ microglia displayed an activated state with coordinated upregulation of complement (C1QA/B/C) and phagocytic genes and downregulation of homeostatic markers (P2RY12, CX3CR1). In ELNI mice exhibiting SCZ-like behaviors, S100A8/S100A9 were upregulated in hippocampus and frontal cortex, accompanied by CD68 induction and reduced synaptophysin, with S100A8 correlating positively with CD68 and negatively with synaptophysin. Molecular docking identified hydroxyzine as a candidate S100A8 ligand. These convergent findings establish S100A8 as a hub linking peripheral immune dysregulation to microglial activation and synaptic pathology in SCZ, highlighting it as a candidate biomarker and therapeutic target.

secondary.title: From pathogenesis to non-medical therapy: A review of exploring sensory and multi-sensory stimulation as a non-invasive treatment approach for Alzheimer's disease.
secondary.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder, marked by the accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques, tau pathology, and synaptic dysfunction, ultimately leading to memory loss, cognitive decline, neuropsychiatric symptoms and neuronal degeneration that impairs daily functioning. Despite the availability of pharmacological treatments developed to slow down symptom progression, their clinical efficacy remains uncertain, and they are frequently associated with adverse side effects, underscoring the urgent demand for safer and more effective therapeutic alternatives. Non-pharmacological approaches, therefore, have been investigated and are considered promising alternative therapeutic strategies for AD. This paper outlines the pathological features and neural network changes that occur across the progression of Alzheimer's disease (AD), reviews the effects of different sensory stimulation approaches on reducing these AD-associated changes, and discusses the potential mechanisms underlying various sensory and multisensory stimulation interventions in mitigating AD-related symptoms. These sensory stimulation interventions, including 40 Hz Gamma Entrainment Using Sensory Stimulation [GENUS], Photobiomodulation, Bright Light Therapy, Music Therapy, Aromatherapy, Tactile Stimulation, and Multisensory Stimulation, are found to slow down the progression of AD by ameliorating multiple AD pathologies, enhancing cognitive function, promoting neuroplasticity, regulating sleep patterns, and reducing behavioural or neuropsychiatric symptoms. Crucially, this present work integrates both human and animal studies, aligning clinical outcomes with mechanistic insights derived from animal studies, thereby bridging preclinical and clinical research to promote the translation of sensory interventions into effective treatments for patients with AD.

secondary.title: Behavioral pharmacology of isolated cannabidiol in animal models of autism spectrum disorder: a systematic review.
secondary.abstract: RATIONALE: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is characterized by differences and challenges in social communication and interaction, restricted and repetitive behaviors, and variable cognitive alterations. Cannabidiol (CBD), a non-psychoactive phytocannabinoid with a complex pharmacological profile, has been investigated in preclinical models of ASD, particularly regarding its behavioral and neurobiological effects. OBJECTIVES: To systematically evaluate the behavioral effects of isolated cannabidiol in animal models of ASD and examine associated neurobiological correlates relevant to central nervous system function. METHODS: A systematic search was conducted in eight electronic databases without date restriction. Preclinical studies assessing isolated CBD in animal models of ASD were included. Owing to methodological heterogeneity, data were synthesized according to the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) guideline, with behavioral outcomes defined as primary endpoints and neurobiological measures as secondary outcomes. The review protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251003869). RESULTS: Nine studies met the inclusion criteria, predominantly using rodent models, especially valproic acid-induced ASD, as well as zebrafish larvae and one behavioral ASD-like rat model. CBD produced dose-, model-, and treatment-regimen-dependent improvements in repetitive behavior, social interaction, recognition memory, and locomotor hyperactivity. Anxiolytic-like effects were inconsistently reported. Behavioral modulation was accompanied by changes in neurobiological markers, including CB1 receptor expression, parvalbumin-positive interneuron density, oxidative/nitrosative stress parameters, and qualitative neuroanatomical and cellular alterations in brain regions implicated in ASD-related behaviors. However, sex-specific effects could not be adequately assessed because most rodent studies used only males, zebrafish studies were conducted at larval stages, and mixed-sex data were not stratified. CONCLUSIONS: Evidence from animal models suggests that isolated CBD exerts promising but heterogeneous behavioral effects in ASD-relevant paradigms, supported by neurobiological changes that may help explain some behavioral outcomes. However, substantial methodological variability, limited sex-specific analyses, and incomplete reporting of bias-control procedures limit certainty, highlighting the need for more rigorous preclinical studies addressing dose-response relationships, mechanisms, sex as a biological variable, safety, long-term outcomes, and translational relevance.

secondary.title: Oxidative stress in neurodegeneration: from a simple insult to a dynamic regulator.
secondary.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the central role of oxidative stress in neurodegenerative diseases, and to explore its dynamic regulatory features, underlying signaling pathways, and molecular mechanisms, as well as advanced technological strategies for antioxidant intervention. METHODS: This review comprehensively evaluated existing literature on oxidative stress in neurodegenerative diseases. It analyzed key regulatory pathways (Nrf2, Keap1, AMPK, mTOR) and molecular processes, including ferroptosis, NETosis, and mitochondrial quality control systems, along with oxidative damage to DNA, lipids, and proteins. The review also assessed advanced technological approaches such as subcellular organelle targeting, nanocarrier delivery systems (e.g. gold nanoparticles, liposomes for glutathione delivery), and single-cell/spatial omics technologies (e.g. single-cell redoxomics, spatial transcriptomics). RESULTS: Oxidative stress exhibits dynamic features, generating protective signals in early stages but transitioning into destructive factors later. A major obstacle for current antioxidant therapies is the blood-brain barrier. Breakthrough strategies identified include precision targeting at the subcellular level, functionalized nanoparticles for efficient antioxidant delivery, and the integration of single-cell redoxomics with spatial transcriptomics to identify specific biomarkers and enable personalized treatments. DISCUSSION: By integrating novel molecular mechanisms and advanced technological resources, this review redefines oxidative stress not as a singular event but as a complex, dynamically regulated system in neurodegenerative diseases. This reconceptualization provides new perspectives for developing targeted and personalized therapeutic interventions.

secondary.title: iPSC-derived retinal organoids: Biological insights and progress toward photoreceptor replacement therapy.
secondary.abstract: Induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived retinal organoids (ROs) have emerged as a platform for photoreceptor replacement therapy, supported by two complementary approaches: cone precursor cell transplantation and RO transplantation. Both have demonstrated proof of concept for functional synaptic integration with the host retinal network, with the first clinical application of iPSC-derived RO transplantation conducted in 2020. Key mechanistic insights include the role of the host environment in cone integration, genome editing-based enhancement of host-graft synaptogenesis recapitulating developmental synaptic assembly, and synaptic rewiring capacity in the adult primate retina. Beyond biology, successful clinical translation requires establishing meaningful endpoints that reflect stepwise therapeutic improvement, scalable good manufacturing practice (GMP)-compliant manufacturing including validated preservation protocols, and regulatory frameworks accommodating progenitor-stage cell therapies. Together, these advances offer a realistic path toward vision restoration in patients with currently untreatable retinal degenerative diseases.

secondary.title: Multi-omics integration deciphers arsenic-induced multi-organ toxicity and the novel ferroptosis axis.
secondary.abstract: Chronic arsenic exposure threatens over 200 million people worldwide and induces multi-organ injury, yet the panoramic molecular reprogramming across organs remains incompletely understood, and traditional single-omics approaches fail to capture cross-level and cross-organ regulatory associations. This review systematically integrates evidence from global epidemiology to single-cell spatial omics, tracing the evolution of multi-omics technologies-from single-platform profiling to data fusion strategies such as coupled matrix factorization (CMF) and the DIABLO framework, two complementary multi-omics integration approaches-and to cutting-edge spatial transcriptomics. We highlight ferroptosis as a common mechanism in arsenic-induced multi-organ injury. At the molecular level, we propose a mechanistic model wherein arsenic (AsIII) disrupts selenium metabolism by inhibiting Sec-tRNASec synthesis, thereby impairing selenoprotein (especially GPX4) biosynthesis, a paradigm distinct from the traditional "ROS burst → lipid peroxidation" theory. Supporting evidence includes reduced 75Se incorporation into cellular RNA, genetic deletion of PRDX6 exacerbating ferroptosis, and rescue by selenium supplementation via Nrf2 activation. At the organ level, we compare toxicity features and propose that tissue-intrinsic ferroptosis thresholds-determined by iron content, PUFA-phospholipid composition, GSH reserves, GPX4 redundancy, and selenium availability-govern differential organ susceptibility; the brain shows extreme vulnerability, whereas the liver exhibits relative resistance. Emerging spatial omics further reveals elevated arsenic-responsive gene expression in tumor-adjacent regions. This systems toxicology paradigm offers mechanistic grounding for combinatorial biomarker panels and genotype-guided precision selenium supplementation, although definitive causal validation through tissue-specific Gpx4 knockout or Sec-tRNASec rescue experiments remains a critical next step. We also discuss prospects for AI-driven toxicity prediction models.

secondary.title: Human iPSC models of myocardial infarction: From injury to repair and therapeutic discovery.
secondary.abstract: Myocardial infarction (MI) remains a leading cause of death worldwide, and therapies that limit injury, promote repair, and restore cardiac function remain limited. Human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) provide a renewable source of patient-specific cardiac cells and have enabled the development of increasingly complex in vitro models that incorporate cardiomyocytes together with supporting stromal and vascular cell types. These models are now being used to study multiple stages of MI pathophysiology and are increasingly being applied in therapeutic discovery and regenerative strategies. In this review, we summarize hiPSC-based cardiac models spanning 2D cultures to advanced 3D tissues, organoids, and heart-on-chip systems, evaluating how well they capture key features of human MI. We further discuss hiPSC applications in therapeutic discovery, drug screening, precision medicine, and regenerative repair. Finally, we highlight priorities for the field, including improved physiological complexity, stronger translational robustness, bioengineering strategies, and integration with multi-omics.

papers.title: Pathogenic MAPK8IP3 variants drive distinct motor and behavioral phenotypes in humans and mice
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Pathogenic variants in MAPK8IP3 (JIP3) cause Neurodevelopmental Disorder with or without variable Brain Abnormalities (NEDBA), characterized by cognitive impairment, global developmental delay, motor dysfunction, abnormal muscle tone, behavioral dysregulation including autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), seizures, and structural brain abnormalities. While more than 30 largely de novo MAPK8IP3 variants have been reported, the functional impact of variants across JIP3 protein structural domains is poorly defined. To address this knowledge gap, we compare clinical features of individuals with a truncating (p.E27X) or one of two missense (p.R578C and p.R1146C) variants from distinct JIP3 functional protein domains to corresponding knock-in mouse models. Our findings showed that all individuals, regardless of variant type, exhibited delays in language and gross motor function, but individual variants were associated with distinct motor, cognitive, and psychiatric symptoms. Corresponding homozygous p.E27X and p.R1147C variant mice resulted in embryonic lethality, consistent with essential roles for JIP3 in early neurodevelopment. Behavioral characterization of viable heterozygous mice revealed variant-specific locomotor, motor coordination, and hindlimb clasping defects that closely recapitulate clinical observations. Heterozygous p.R579C mice exhibited reduced locomotion, impaired motor performance, and hypertonia-like clasping, mirroring human motor deficits. In contrast, p.R1147C mice displayed hyperactivity, hindlimb clasping, and decreased brain weight, paralleling human clinical features. Together, our findings demonstrate that while distinct MAPK8IP3 variants lead to some shared phenotypes, they are also associated with distinct phenotypes that could reveal domain-specific aspects of JIP3 function. This work establishes the first domain-resolved in vivo rodent models of NEDBA and provides a validated translational platform for mechanistic investigation and preclinical therapeutic testing.

papers.title: Parkinson's disease genetic risk converges on Lewy body pathology-associated microglial states
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) and related α-synucleinopathies are defined by the spread of Lewy body (LB) pathology across vulnerable brain regions, yet how substantia nigra (SN) myeloid cells respond remains unresolved. Using SOX10-based oligodendrocyte depletion and CD11b-based myeloid enrichment, we profiled 169,799 brain myeloid cells and nuclei from 96 donors spanning the LB continuum, including 86,427 from the SN, and integrated them with AMP PD for a total of 298,592 profiles. Across eight conserved states, α-synucleinopathy is associated with a bidirectional signature: upregulated glycolytic and proteostatic-stress programs alongside downregulated lysosomal and mitochondrial pathways. Microglia shift from P2RY12-high sensome cells toward an HSP90AA1-high proteostatic stress state, a transition that intensifies at late Braak LB stages. Immunohistochemistry confirmed that HSP60+ proteostatic microglia state proportions increase with SN neuron loss. A rare NUCKS1-high state (~1% of myeloid cells), more abundant in late-stage disease, carried the strongest PD polygenic-risk loading. The PD-protective rs3732765-A allele, a microglial cis-eQTL that lowers P2RY12 expression, was nominally associated with a higher proportion of P2RY12-high microglia and higher lysosomal program activity. These findings frame microglial involvement as structured and genetically tractable, nominating the P2RY12 genetic axis and NUCKS1-high microglia for mechanistic studies.

papers.title: KIF1A-driven entry of degradative lysosomes into the axon is developmentally regulated by the microtubule environment at the axon initial segment
papers.abstract: Neuronal function requires precise transport of lysosomal vesicles along highly polarized processes, yet how this trafficking is spatially and developmentally regulated remains poorly understood. Here, we show that the neuronally enriched kinesin-3 motor KIF1A is required for dendritic and axonal localization of lysosomal vesicles in both immature and mature rat hippocampal neurons. Remarkably, the specialized microtubule environment of the axon initial segment (AIS) restricts KIF1A-driven transport of degradative, cathepsin D-positive lysosomal vesicles while permitting less degradative lysosomal vesicles to enter axons in mature neurons. Disrupting the AIS microtubule environment or expressing a hereditary spastic paraplegia type 30-associated KIF1A variant with increased affinity for GTP-tubulin bypasses this restriction, enabling degradative lysosomal vesicles to enter mature axons. In human iPSC-derived neurons, KIF1A depletion similarly disrupts axonal lysosomal vesicle transport, causes autophagic vesicle accumulation, and triggers axonal degeneration. Together, our findings reveal a developmentally regulated AIS gate that selectively controls KIF1A-driven lysosomal vesicle transport into axons and link its subversion to KIF1A-associated neurological disease.

papers.title: Dysregulation of miR-103a-3p/AGFG1 axis links endocytic trafficking dysfunction to ER stress in Parkinson’s disease
papers.abstract: Background Parkinson’s disease is defined by progressive dopaminergic neurodegeneration and α-synuclein pathology. Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and clathrin-mediated endocytosis dysfunction are implicated in disease pathogenesis, but the molecular mechanisms connecting these processes remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate a miR-103a-3p/AGFG1 axis as a regulator link between endocytic trafficking and ER stress in Parkinson’s disease. Methods MiR-103a-3p and AGFG1 were examined in plasma and postmortem substantia nigra from patients with Parkinson’s disease and controls. Gain-and loss-of-function studies, target validation and live-cell imaging were used to define the role of the miR-103a-3p/AGFG1 axis in ER stress and endocytic trafficking. The pathway was further investigated in SNCA A53T and LRRK2 G2019S hiPSC-derived neurons. Therapeutic targeting of AGFG1 was evaluated using antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) in vitro and in a 6-hydroxydopamine mouse model. Results MiR-103a-3p was significantly reduced in Parkinson’s disease plasma and substantia nigra, whereas AGFG1 was increased in nigral tissue. MiR-103a-3p directly repressed AGFG1 and attenuated thapsigargin-induced ER stress, while miR-103a-3p inhibition or AGFG1 overexpression exacerbated stress signalling. AGFG1 knockdown reversed the effects of miR-103a-3p inhibition, establishing AGFG1 as a functional downstream effector. Mechanistically, AGFG1 associated and co-trafficked with clathrin-positive vesicles, whereas ER stress progressively disrupted AGFG1-clathrin vesicle dynamics, revealing an association between endocytic trafficking and stress signalling. In genetic Parkinson’s disease models, SNCA A53T and LRRK2 G2019S neurons showed mutation-dependent differences in AGFG1 expression and stress regulation. eIF2α phosphorylation increased in both SNCA A53T and LRRK2 G2019S neurons, whereas AGFG1 and GADD34 upregulation was selective to SNCA A53T neurons. Importantly, ASO-mediated AGFG1 suppression attenuated ER stress in vitro and preserved nigral dopaminergic neurons with improved motor performance in vivo . Conclusion Our findings identify the miR-103a-3p/AGFG1 axis as a previously unrecognised molecular link between endocytic trafficking dysfunction and ER stress in Parkinson’s disease, and support AGFG1 as a mechanistically potential therapeutic target.

papers.title: Proteomic clocks reveal organ-specific signatures of aging in mice
papers.abstract: Aging alters protein abundance throughout the body, but whether proteomic aging signatures are shared across organs, and how they are represented in RNA, remains unclear. Plasma proteomics does not measure protein abundance directly within individual organs. Here, we developed organ-specific proteomic aging clocks for eight mouse organs. The clocks retained age associations across independent cohorts but transferred poorly between organs of the same mice, indicating predominantly organ-specific aging signatures. This organ specificity extended to RNA. Applied to the transcriptomes of the genes encoding each clock's protein features, with protein-derived weights unchanged, the scores retained age associations in independent transcriptomic cohorts, with stronger associations in the corresponding organs. The strength of age associations across molecular layers also differed by organ: in paired analysis, protein scores tracked age more strongly than RNA scores in brain and skeletal muscle, with no statistically detectable difference in kidney, liver or lung, suggesting a greater post-transcriptional contribution to proteomic aging in brain and muscle. In spatial transcriptomes, protein-derived RNA scores rose with age within tissue niches, usually without detectable changes in relative niche abundance. In the brain, white matter and glia-enriched microdomains showed elevated proteomic scores compared to other regions since young age. Together, these findings support organ-specific regulation of proteomic aging and identify molecular remodeling within persistent tissue compartments.

papers.title: TMEM55B promotes anterograde transport and distal axonal distribution of LAMP1-positive organelles
papers.abstract: Lysosomal function throughout life is vital for the proper functioning and survival of post-mitotic neurons by mediating cellular signaling, degradation, and recycling processes. Their intracellular transport relies on microtubule-dependent mechanisms involving kinesin and dynein motors. While lysosomes were long thought absent from axons, recent studies have demonstrated the importance of LAMP1-positive endo-/lysosomal organelles in axonal compartments. This study investigates the physiological role of TMEM55B, a lysosomal membrane protein involved in lysosome positioning and motor coupling in neurons. TMEM55B is highly expressed in LAMP1-positive organelles in cortical neurons. We generated viable Tmem55b knockout mice that exhibited altered lysosomal positioning in neurons. Lysosomes clustered abnormally in the pre-axonal exclusion zone and the proximal axon, with many forming elongated tubular structures. Similarly, in primary rat neurons, TMEM55B depletion resulted in lysosomal tubulation and impaired bidirectional lysosomal transport, particularly in distal axon segments, without affecting lysosome velocity in the proximal and mid-axon. These transport defects were consistent with disrupted JIP4 function, a scaffold linking TMEM55B to both dynein and kinesin motors. TMEM55B deficiency did not result in neurodegeneration, behavioral deficits, or reduced lifespan in mice. As an orthogonal approach, we analyzed TMEM55B function in C. elegans. Worms lacking the TMEM55B homolog Y71H2AM.2 showed altered lysosomal dynamics in cholinergic neurons, supporting an evolutionarily conserved role. To test the involvement of TMEM55B's paralog, TMEM55A, in regulating neuronal lysosome positioning, we generated Tmem55a/b double-knockout mice, which exhibit impaired growth, premature death, and an overall aggravated phenotype. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that both TMEM55B and TMEM55A regulate lysosome distribution in neurons, particularly in axons, by influencing JIP4-dependent retro- and, notably, anterograde motor protein-mediated transport. This function is critical for spatial lysosomal homeostasis. Our study underscores the importance of TMEM55A/TMEM55B in regulating neuronal organelle dynamics and may be a factor considered in neurodegenerative diseases involving lysosomal trafficking defects.

papers.title: COG5-mediated Golgi organization coordinates neural progenitor fate during human brain development
papers.abstract: Apical radial glial cells (aRGs) are highly polarized epithelial cells that drive human cortical development through tightly regulated lineage progression. A distinctive feature of aRGs is their non-canonical Golgi organization, raising the possibility that specialized intracellular trafficking and secretory processes contribute to progenitor behaviour. However, how Golgi architecture contributes to human corticogenesis remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate this question in the context of COG5 deficiency, a rare congenital disorder of glycosylation associated with neurodevelopmental defects, using patient-derived fibroblasts and brain organoids, N-glycomics, glycolipidomics, and single-cell transcriptomics. We show that COG5 deficiency disrupts Golgi organization and impairs Golgi-to-ER retrograde trafficking. At the neurodevelopmental level, COG5-deficient organoids display altered ventricular organization and reduced basal progenitor abundance. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis reveals rewired developmental trajectories characterized by premature differentiation from apical progenitors with activation of neuronal pathways. Despite the absence of major abnormalities in plasma glycoproteins glycosylation, glycolipidomic analysis identified marked defects in glycosphingolipid maturation within patient-derived brain organoids, indicating selective impairment of neural lipid glycosylation. Transcriptomic and biochemical analyses further revealed dysregulation of developmental pathways, including reduced Notch signalling and altered localization of both cleaved Notch1 and the Golgi-associated protein ACBD3. Consistent with impaired progenitor maintenance, COG5-deficient organoids displayed altered cleavage plane orientation in apical progenitors. Together, our findings suggest a link between Golgi organization, intracellular trafficking, membrane glycosylation, and lineage progression in human neural progenitors, identifying Golgi architecture as an important regulator of apical radial glial cell biology and cortical development.

papers.title: Generation of human iPSC-derived motor neurons with defined regional identities across the rostrocaudal axis
papers.abstract: This study establishes a unified pipeline for generating human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived motor neurons (iMNs) with defined hindbrain, cervical, and lumbar identities to support anatomically resolved studies of motor neuron development and degeneration. Conventional differentiation methods can efficiently produce iMNs but provide limited control over rostrocaudal identity and frequently generate populations with heterogeneous HOX profiles. We addressed this limitation by optimizing developmental morphogen combinations and treatment windows, establishing three complementary protocols that reproducibly generated hindbrain/rhombomere-associated motor neurons (RiMNs), cervical motor neurons (CiMNs), and lumbar motor neurons (LiMNs) across iPSC lines from six non-diseased donors balanced by sex. Transcriptomic and protein analyses demonstrated graded rostrocaudal specification from RiMNs through CiMNs to LiMNs, together with region-appropriate motor neuron subtype features. These identities showed the expected relationships to human week 9 fetal rostrocaudal HOX programs. High-density multielectrode array analysis further revealed synchronized network firing, electrically active neurite networks, and enhanced axonal signal propagation in the regional iMN populations compared with conventionally differentiated iMNs. Spike-sorted recordings additionally revealed protocol-associated differences in single-neuron electrophysiological profiles. Together, this three-protocol pipeline enables the reproducible generation and comparative analysis of anatomically defined human motor neuron populations and provides region-matched cellular models for investigating motor neuron development, selective degeneration, and therapeutic responses.

papers.title: Sex and autism share cell type-specific effects on cortical gene expression
papers.abstract: Potent sex effects on the prevalence and presentation of autism could theoretically reflect overlapping neurobiology, but tests in brain gene expression have so far been limited to bulk tissue - overlooking cell type heterogeneity. Here, we use newly available single-nucleus RNA-sequencing datasets, to test if regional, cell type-specific sex effects on gene expression overlap with those of autism (using schizophrenia as a comparison condition). Cellular gene expression effects were estimated for sex across six cortical regions (169 samples, 30 individuals), and for autism (63 individuals, 33 cases), and schizophrenia (140 individuals, 65 cases) in frontal cortex. Genes with significant sex effects showed a stronger overlap with those differentially expressed in autism than schizophrenia. Multivariate analyses revealed a significant shared axis of transcriptomic effects between sex and autism (but not schizophrenia). This axis featured a protein-protein interaction network enriched for autism risk genes and synaptic biology, downregulated in autism across cell types, and female biased in fusiform neurons, but male biased in angular gyrus glial cells. Thus, the autism transcriptomic signatures in frontal cortex show cell type- and region-specific alignments with sex effects on gene expression - pointing to a complexity in overlaps that informs theoretical models of sex modulation of autism liability.

papers.title: TMEM55B downregulation promotes neurodegeneration in Alzheimer’s disease models
papers.abstract: Lysosomal distribution is critical for numerous biological functions within the cell, including protein degradation in autophagosomes, cholesterol homeostasis, and cell invasion. Changes in the positioning of lysosomes and dysregulation of lysosomal trafficking are known to contribute to different human pathologies, such as lysosomal storage disease, neurodegeneration, and cancer. Here we report the critical role of the lysosomal T ransmembrane P rotein 55B (TMEM55B) in mediating neurodegeneration. Using human clinical-pathological datasets, transgenic flies and iPSC-derived neurons, we demonstrate that loss of function of dTMEM55 potentiates neuronal degeneration. We found that TMEM55B levels are lowered in severe Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) cases, validated from microarray, single neuron and total RNA Seq datasets from brain sections of the ROSMAP cohort. Our results demonstrates that loss of function of dTMEM55 results in accumulation of lysosomes in the fly’s larval neuronal axons, enhances Tau-mediated retinal degeneration, locomotory dysfunction, lethality, and cell death in the fly AD model. The iPSC-derived AD neurons exhibit reduced TMEM55B levels, autophagic flux defects and increased accumulation of phosphorylated Tau in the lysosomes, confirming the observations in the fly. Overall, our findings indicate that TMEM55B downregulation could contribute to neurodegeneration through defects in lysosomal transport, potentially hindering autophagic clearance of Tau. Our findings have significant relevance in validating the role of lysosomal proteins in normal lysosomal function and maintaining healthy neurons. This work supports continued research into lysosome-mediated neurodegeneration and may provide a basis for exploring potential therapeutic approaches for lysosome-associated neuronal disorders. Highlights TMEM55B expression is significantly reduced in postmortem brain tissues of patients with severe AD. Genetic loss of TMEM55B enhances Tau-mediated neurodegeneration in Drosophila , indicating a conserved neuroprotective function. TMEM55B regulates neuronal lysosomal positioning across species, and its loss disrupts lysosomal transport. iPSC-derived Alzheimer’s disease neurons exhibit late-stage TMEM55B downregulation concomitant with increased accumulation of pathological phosphorylated Tau. papers.title: Cellular context defines brain-specific functions of genes associated with neurodevelopmental disorders
papers.abstract: Differential gene expression rarely explains why certain genes, e.g. associated with tissue-specific manifestations of human disease, exert tissue-specific functions. To understand how gene expression and molecular context act in concert to drive tissue-specific gene function, we focus on Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), for which underlying disease mechanisms are still poorly understood. We developed a computational framework that harmonizes and integrates spatiotemporal transcriptome datasets enabling us to systematically quantify preferential gene expression across tissues and developmental stages. Applying this pipeline to approximately 1,000 NDD-associated genes, we find that only about 10% show brain-preferential expression, with distinct gene clusters instead exhibiting significant upregulation in non-brain tissues. Investigation of these clusters reveals regulatory mechanisms that govern mitochondrial function to meet neurons’ high energetic demands, which are mechanistically distinct from those employed by other energy-intensive tissues such as heart and skeletal muscle. Furthermore, by integrating tissue-agnostic protein-protein interaction data with our expression resource, we identify putative brain-specific interaction partners for 22 uniformly expressed NDD-associated genes. We experimentally validate these interactions for QRICH1 and demonstrate that disease-associated mutations disrupt them, providing a molecular hypothesis for how QRICH1 acquires brain-specific function and how its disruption might cause Ververi-Brady syndrome. Together, our findings highlight the importance of molecular context for brain-specific gene function in the context of neurodevelopmental disease. We provide a framework for dissecting molecular mechanisms of tissue-specific Mendelian-like disorders and for exploring how biological processes are adapted to tissue-specific needs.

papers.title: Dishevelled2 Condensates control Axon Initial Segment (AIS) assembly and function through MTCL1-Dependent microtubule recruitment
papers.abstract: SUMMARY In the epithelium, Planar Cell Polarity (PCP) signaling coordinates cellular organization along the plane of the tissue, perpendicular to the apicobasal axis. In neurons, polarity is instead expressed through the structural and molecular asymmetry that separates the axon from the somatodendritic compartment. Core PCP proteins are essential for neuronal development and function, and have been linked to neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism spectrum disorders and epilepsy. However, their precise roles in the establishment of neuronal polarity remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify Dishevelled2 (Dvl2), a central PCP signaling scaffold, as a novel component of the axon initial segment (AIS), the proximal axonal domain that maintains neuronal polarity and initiates action potentials. We show that Dvl2 defines, both in vivo and in cultured hippocampal neurons, a proximal subdomain positioned upstream of the major AIS marker Ankyrin-G (Ank-G) and is closely associated with microtubule bundles. Dvl2 is already detected during early axon specification, suggesting that it participates in the initial organization of the proximal axon. Functional depletion of Dvl proteins disrupts AIS architecture, reduces the accumulation of Ankyrin-G and other core AIS components, and impairs the organization of AIS microtubule bundles. These structural defects translate into altered neuronal excitability, with a reduced AIS-dependent component of the action potential. Mechanistically, we identify MTCL1 as a microtubule-associated partner that recruits Dvl2 from biomolecular condensate assemblies onto microtubules. This recruitment requires the DIX and PDZ domains of Dvl2. Notably, selective intracellular binders targeting the Dvl2 PDZ domain perturb Dvl2 condensate organization and compromise AIS formation. Together, our data identify Dvl2 as an organizer of the proximal AIS and reveal a Dvl2-MTCL1-dependent mechanism coupling condensate scaffolding, microtubule organization, and neuronal excitability. papers.title: PDE4D inhibition activates cAMP-PKA signaling to preserve mitochondrial homeostasis and prevent neuronal necroptosis in Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: Abstract Alzheimer’s disease involves progressive necroptosis of neurons, and the associated cognitive deficits can be mitigated by inhibiting cAMP-degrading phosphodiesterase 4D (PDE4D). Here we explored whether and how PDE4D may be involved in neuronal necroptosis in the disease. Knocking down PDE4D in two mouse models significantly improved learning and memory, while reducing Aβ 1−42 deposition and tau phosphorylation. APPswe/PS1ΔE9 transgenic mice(APP/PS1 mice) or the 3⋅TG mutations in mice upregulated PDE4D and pro-necroptotic proteins RIPK1, MLKL and STING, while downregulating the neuronal marker PSD95; knocking down PDE4D in hippocampus reversed these pathogenic changes. Inhibiting PDE4D in cultures of HT22 hippocampal neurons antagonized the ability of Aβ 1−42 to induce production of reactive oxygen species, mitochondrial membrane depolarization, mitochondrial fragmentation and necroptosis. Inhibiting mitochondrial fission using the Drp1 inhibitor Mdivi-1 or activating protein kinase A with 8-CPT-cAMP led to similar effects as inhibiting PDE4D. The opposite effects were observed when cultures were treated with the STING agonist SR717, the autophagy inhibitor 3-methyladenine, or protein kinase A inhibitor H89. Our experiments suggest that inhibiting PDE4D in neurons may alleviate cognitive defects in Alzheimer's disease by upregulating levels of cAMP, which in turn stimulates protein kinase A to protect mitochondria from fragmentation and promote mitophagy, thereby preventing necroptosis.
